en: Preface to the Collated Edition of the *Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*:
Profound Meaning and Textual Commentary I have heard that the teaching of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* serves to sustain the life-force of the eternal abiding.

Yet, if one’s blood and qi are flourishing and the internal organs are robust, such that the six seasonal influences strike in alternation and the five flavors interact in harmony, this is merely sufficient to nourish the physical body.
What destiny must be sustained? When it reaches its decline, wind, rain, mist, and dew invade from without, while bitter, sour, grief, and pain wound from within.
When the liver and spleen are disturbed and the internal organs are overwhelmed, cold and heat intensify.

To expel the pathogenic influences and support the vital essence, preserving the years like ice and jade—were it not for the wondrous *agada* elixir, nothing could provide such succor. This is comparable to the Buddha’s sun shining from on high.
When the mountains are leveled and the plains made even, and at the time when the sun is at its zenith and casts no shadow, the Dharma will flourish with brilliant splendor;
how then could one worry that the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvitendriya*) would not continue?

In this degenerate and turbid age, when people are prone to falling into false views, you have maintained purity—unlike those who, like victims of a famine, are beset by thieves and left destitute and ill. You must urgently grasp it with a mind of focused intensity and humble vigilance.
Gently drawing forth the withered Dharma-body, when stretched it stands solitary and desolate; when relaxed, it is vast and expansive.

At such a time, one must first restrain and stabilize the faculties, partaking of the nectar of the teachings to sustain the life of wisdom; were it not for upholding the Vinaya and discussing the Eternal, no merit could be achieved.
This teaching receives those of heterodox views and guides the small-minded, leading them gradually into the Sudden, while simultaneously manifesting impermanence.

Yet, by cultivating this practice, all that is constant, continuous, and variegated converges within the eternal celestial net; like the light of a thousand lamps, there is no subtle detail not fully present and no entity not harmoniously integrated.

Thus, from the smallest speck of dust to divine beings and insects, from the minute to the vast, and from the heterodox to the orthodox, it enables even those who are solitary and suffering to all wear the talisman of longevity. This is the supreme essential *agada* medicine.
Everything here is for the purpose of rescuing an age of decline. Zhiyan of Zhang’an thought only of quenching his thirst with nectar;

entering the mountains and tracing the rivers, he was like a blind man longing for a dog—his resolve never ceasing, he extensively sought out ancient commentaries. Sitting upon arrow-straw mats in the dark forests, he underwent every kind of hardship until he finally completed his profound commentary (*Xuanshu*).
That he acted in this way was nothing other than to rescue an age of decline. Master Xian, observing the faculties of people in these later and inferior times...

With meager talent and narrow understanding, I rely upon this scripture; yet its profound commentary is so obscure that it is like facing a direction one cannot discern—this alone would cause one to weep at the fork of the road.

Thus, my annotations and critiques of the great sections are nothing other than attempts to rescue an age in decline. As for the sentences, they belong to the realm of "nothingness," and as for the commentary, it is cast upon those who practice meditation.
There has never been anyone more confused than I, until there appeared the Great Monk Shouda, who early on bathed in the King’s Spring.

Liu Yan held the *Yingluo zhu jiao guan* (The Pearl Necklace Teaching for Contemplation) as profoundly comprehensive and its commentaries as exceedingly rich; beholding this sub-commentary, his sighs of admiration were unending.

Consequently, he restored the original text to clear the old grievance, dividing it into sections and distilling its essence. Although Master [Zhi]hui had passed away, those who continued his resolve were many, and their efforts in collating and verifying the text became increasingly diligent.

Thus, the Song and Ming editions lacked nothing that was not examined; the connection proceeds from the sub-commentary (*shu*) to the root text (*xuan*), and from the root text to the individual phrases (*ju*).
The lost sheep was sought until its recovery at Hengchuan; the *Jizhuzi* (Chicken’s Foot) manuscript was obtained and entrusted to me for collation.
As for this book, is it not like gold found in the Jambū River? Now that it is being published, I venture to inform the students of the Dharma:
the reason the many eminent scholars have exerted themselves toward this scripture is none other than to rescue an age of decline. Today, the era of decline has reached its ultimate limit. Alas!
While those suffering from illness tread upon one another and join arms in distress, this wondrous and excellent medicine—ground, sifted, and compounded—is right here before us.
Yet, being unwilling to take it, they bring an untimely end to their precious life-force; how can this compare to the profound and painstaking efforts of the Buddhas and the patriarchs of old?
In the second month of spring in the *Kwansei* year of the *Jinshi* cycle,
the Provisional Head of the Monastic Order, Jitō, respectfully prefaces these rules of compilation.
Originally, the *Xuanyi* consisted of two fascicles and the *Wenju* one fascicle;

since the present combined edition (*huiben*) also consists of two fascicles, the *Xuanyi* contains headings at the end of each fascicle as well as upper and lower subheadings, whereas the *Wenju* does not.

I have retained these original features entirely, distinguishing between the *Xuanyi* and the *Wenju* merely by raising or lowering a single character. This combined edition was personally titled by me.

An ancient catalogue states that there was a single fascicle titled *Nirvāṇa Xuanyi Wenzu* (The Profound Meaning and Textual Analysis of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) composed by Daoxian, but its text had long been lost.

Now, fortunately, it has been recovered; having read it, I am certain it was indeed his composition. Nevertheless, as the original manuscript does not list the author, I do not dare to attribute it here.
The original text of the *Wenju* (Explanatory Text) initially bears the title "Wenju," while at its conclusion it is titled "Chao" (Extracts); I dare not alter this.
Regarding the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), there are four editions for collation—the Mingzang edition, the Wazang edition, the Jiyao edition, and a manuscript of an ancient edition.
Since the Ming edition is the most excellent among them, I have followed the Ming edition throughout; where there are variant readings, they are noted above.
It is labeled as "The Harmony" (Wawa), which is the original manuscript; as "The Essential Pivot" (Yōki), which is the essential version;
and as "A Single Copy of the Ancient Manuscript" (I-sha kohon). However, since only those that are correct need to be preserved, I shall not further elaborate on those that are certainly incorrect.
As for the text, I have currently obtained only a single copy, which is indeed an ancient artifact.

It is regrettable that it contains many additions, omissions, and errors, and furthermore, there is no other version available for collation. I have now humbly appended my observations based on the narrow view through a tube;
I request that those who obtain a superior edition in the future will correct this work.

A character raised one level signifies the profound meaning (xuan-yi); a character lowered one level signifies the words and phrases (wen-ju). As for the symbol △, it signifies a topical division (ke).
However, where there is a topical division but no commentary, marking it separately would be too pedantic; therefore, these are now included following the main body of the text.

Regarding the phrasing and topical headings, whether they are present or absent, detailed or concise at the beginning or end, and whether they are integrated with the explanatory text such that they cannot be separated for independent circulation, or separable when circulated independently but not when integrated—this is because the author did not originally intend for them to be separated or integrated.
If one were to arrange the text according to its meaning, it would not fit perfectly; thus, [the text] is now unified.
I have followed the original text word for word, neither adding nor subtracting, nor altering the sequence.
Where there were omissions or abbreviations, I have either supplemented or elaborated upon them within the grid; however, as these are now easily visible, I have not marked them further.
If the reader can maintain the continuity from beginning to end without losing sight of the distinct shifts in the flow of the composition, they will likely avoid the error of fragmenting the text.
The text contains many errors and omissions; however, fearing that I might inadvertently alter or add to it, I have not dared to emend them.
Yet, where there are omissions in the topical divisions (*ke-yǔ*), they hinder the structural analysis; therefore, I have ventured to supplement them, marking them separately from the original text.
The Combined Text of the Profound Meaning and Word Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
Volume One: The Profound Meaning and Word Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume One.
Compiled by the Sui dynasty Tiantai śramaṇa Guanding. △ Explanation of the Title:
The five meanings [of the title] are identical to those in the *Fahua xuanyi*; they differ only in being an expanded or abbreviated application.

Since that [work] explains them extensively and this one does so concisely, there is no loss of meaning, as the two sutras share the same single flavor (*ekarasa*). Regarding the text, there are two parts: first, [the title]. [Note: The provided text contains a section marker (△) and a structural outline (I.1), which have been translated accordingly.]
A Brief Explanation of the Five Chapters on the Profound Meaning of the Scripture’s Title. Second, from the "Profound Meaning" (*xuanyi*) onwards, the chapters are opened for a detailed explanation.

The first [section] has five parts: (1) A general clarification of phenomena and principle to reveal the meaning of the three virtues; (2) "But the assembly," etc., clarifying the differences between the capacities of beings and the teachings;
(3) "All are the Benevolent One," etc., clarifying the provisional and ultimate nature of the Teacher and how he benefits beings according to what is appropriate; (4) Now... [text continues].
The following section of this great sutra clarifies that the timing of the teaching differs from the five [other] sutras. If this sutra were fully [expounded], the title would be explained in detail;

here, it is briefly interpreted. This initial part further has two sections: first, the direct explanation; second, the conclusion that the Dharma is identical to the analogy. The first of these also has two parts:
first, the designation of the principle-substance of the nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*); second, the explanation starting with "without beginning."
Now, the True Path is profound and tranquil, without beginning and without end; its wondrous principle is empty and mysterious, neither new nor old.
The initial word "now" (*fu*) serves as the opening of the discourse. "The True Path" clarifies the essence of the *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom), which is profound and tranquil;

this clarifies the essence of *nirvāṇa*. The phrase "wondrous principle" below distinguishes its essence: it is empty and mysterious, its measure equal to the *dharmadhātu*; ignorance and birth-and-death are likewise [of this nature].

Thus it is. △ Next, the explanation [of the preceding passage] has two parts: first, a general clarification of phenomena and principle; second, the specific phenomena and principle of this present sutra, beginning with "This sutra...
The first part further has two sections: first, an explanation of the beginning and end; second, an explanation of the new and the old, beginning with "Ignorance..."
To speak of a beginning for that which is beginningless is called ignorance; to speak of an end for that which is endless is precisely the wisdom of all modes (sarvajñatā) and nirvāṇa.
The initial statement regarding a beginning for the beginningless refers to the manifestation of its nature through cultivation, meaning that one observes it with wisdom.

It is because one first recognizes ignorance that it is said to have a beginning but no end; and it is because one speaks of its conclusion in terms of the perfection attained through cultivation that it is said to have an end.
Thus, the "wisdom of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) and "nirvāṇa" pertain to principle (*li*), while "ignorance" and "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*) pertain to phenomena (*shi*).

Furthermore, the wisdom of all modes and nirvāṇa attained through cultivation are phenomena, whereas the wisdom of all modes and nirvāṇa as inherent nature are principle. This is the intended meaning of the text.
I shall explain based solely on the first meaning.
△ From "Because of ignorance" onwards, the text explains the "old" and the "new.

Ignorance is that which has existed from the very beginning of birth and death; it is termed the "old. Perfect Wisdom (Aśeṣajñāna) and Nirvāṇa are that which are attained only through the cultivation of causes; they are termed the "new."
To categorize this as "new" is merely an analogy.

△ Next, from "In this sutra... onwards, there is the main section specifically clarifying the characteristics of the events, principles, causes, and effects of this present sutra, which is divided into four parts. First:
The commentary establishes the beginning and end where there is neither beginning nor end in order to reveal the characteristics of cause and effect.

This sutra, moreover, distinguishes the differences among the three causes of Buddha-nature at the "beginning of what is not a beginning," and further discerns the distinctions among the three virtues of Nirvana as the ultimate fruit at the "end of what is not an end."
Regarding the term "distinction," the phrasing of the commentary follows convenience, yet its meaning is one and the same.
△ Second, from "If the Buddha-nature... onwards, the essence of cause and effect is explained to clarify the new and the old.
If the cause of Buddha-nature were not the cause, and the fruit of Nirvana were not the fruit, then the cause would not differ from the fruit.
If the suchness of the effect is not different from the suchness of the cause, then the suchness of the cessation of nirvāṇa is not the suchness of a newly acquired Buddha-nature,
nor is it newly acquired; likewise, if the suchness of the effect is not different from the suchness of the cause,
the suchness of the Buddha-nature is not the suchness of the cessation of nirvāṇa, nor is it old.
△ 3. "This is then the Buddha-nature" concludes by returning to non-duality.
This means that the suchness (*tathatā*) of the cause and effect of Buddha-nature and *nirvāṇa* is neither new nor old.
△ 4. "Neither new... concludes by establishing the relationship between cultivation and nature (*xiuxing*).
The principle of being neither new nor old is the Dharmakāya; the fruit of being new without being new is Mahāprajñā.

Since there is the perfection of the non-new-and-new *jñāna* (wisdom), the "oldness" that is not new—the afflictions of ignorance and birth-and-death—is ultimately extinguished; this is designated as liberation.
It is also said that phenomena and principle manifest the characteristics of the three bodies (trikāya) and the three virtues (triguṇa). This is the essential purport of the present sutra.
△ Next, "This then... and so forth concludes the section on the identity between the Dharma and the analogy.
This refers to the meaning of the three virtues, which are perfectly complete—neither vertical nor horizontal—like the wonderful letter *i*.

Regarding the phrase "neither vertical nor horizontal": this means that at the time of the cause, the three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, and it is likewise so at the time of the fruit;
thus, the Dharma and the analogy are made subtle and equal.
△ In the section "However, for those of inferior capacity," the second part clarifies the difference between the capacities [of the audience] and the teaching.

However, because the faculties of sentient beings differ—some being sharp and others dull—the teachings of the Great Sage who responds to conditions also distinguish between the sudden and the gradual.
The sudden is likened to the *kṣānti* grass, which yields ghee as soon as the ox eats it; the gradual consists of the five flavors, perfected through successive stages.
Furthermore, there are teaching gates spoken for those with indeterminate faculties and conditions, intended to respond to such specific capacities.
The "sudden" is not like the gradual analogy of placing poison in milk.
As for the statement that there may be "indefiniteness," the single term "indefinite" encompasses both the manifest and the secret meanings of indefiniteness.
Furthermore, it is said that "neither sudden nor gradual" refers to the fact that the indefinite teaching is not restricted exclusively to the sudden or the gradual; thus it is so designated.
The words of "neither-nor.
△ All these are capable of endurance; herein lies the Master of the Three Clarities' [the Buddha’s] appropriateness.

All these are capable of enduring the subtle exhaustion of provisional and ultimate truths, skillfully responding to faculties and conditions to transform others and benefit beings, without the slightest discrepancy.

"Exhaustively elucidating the provisional and the real" means that the provisional is identical to the real and the real is identical to the provisional; thus, one can skillfully respond to and accommodate the suitability of sentient beings. "Sang" (爽) refers to this.
Now, regarding this Great Sūtra, the following four points clarify that the timing of the teaching differs from [the previous]. Among these, the first describes the purpose for which it was taught.
O Disciples, this great sutra is intended to open the way to the gates of the ancient teachings and to reveal the profound, secret meaning of the Tathāgata’s skillful means; therefore,
between the twin śāla trees, the Great Master has uttered this lion's roar.
△ Next, the Master explains the characteristics below.
"Lion's Roar" means definitive teaching; definitive teaching means teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
That the Tathāgata ultimately does not enter *nirvāṇa*—this non-entry into *nirvāṇa* is precisely entry into the Unsurpassed Great [Vehicle].
Riding upon the Great Parinirvāṇa, all may be seen.
△ If this sūtra were complete, there would follow five brief expositions of the title; furthermore, these consist of two parts: first, the direct explanation, and second, "if it were complete."
The following section provides a detailed explanation to clarify the meaning of the title. The first part has two sections; the initial one indicates the two sounds.
If this sutra were translated according to the complete Sanskrit original, it should be called *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The word *mahā* means "great," and *parinirvāṇa* is here translated as "extinction" (*mie-du*).

△ Next, the explanation is divided into two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the reference to the extensive text starting from "The Sūtra" (*sūtra*). Within the direct explanation, there are again two sections: first, the heading and enumeration; second, the detailed exposition.
This explanation of the three characters relies fully upon two meanings: first, the specific (*pṛthak*); second, the general (*sāmānya*).

△ Next, the explanation is divided into two parts: first, the general explanation, and second, the specific application leading to the concluding summary. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the specific explanation, and second, the general explanation.
Regarding the first specific explanation: "Great" refers to the *dharmakāya*; thus, this sutra states: "That which is called 'great' has a nature that is vast."
Vastness is like empty space; its nature is the *dharmatā*, and the *dharmatā* is the *dharmakāya*. "Extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to liberation (*vimukti*);

liberation is the eternal extinction of the two kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). To be free from these sufferings and entanglements of cause and effect is the meaning of liberation.
That which is called "crossing over" (*tāraṇa*) is *mahāprajñā*; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Faith is that which is able to..."

One should know that "entering through wisdom" is that which enables crossing over; the title of this present sutra is specifically marked by three characters, which are alternative names for the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*).
As for the statement that "faith is what enables entry," it is because through possessing great faith one can enter the Buddha-dharma, thereby enabling great wisdom to arise.
It means crossing from this shore of the three delusions and two deaths to reach the further shore of the nirvana of the three virtues.
Second, the general explanation of "Great" refers to the Great Dharma-body, the Great Prajñā, and the Great Liberation.

"Extinction" (nirodha) refers to the fact that these three virtues are all quiescent and extinguished. "Crossing over" (tīrṇa) refers to the fact that these three virtues are all ultimately perfected and complete. Therefore—
The three characters used as the title collectively signify that the three virtues are all the ultimate state of great quiescence.
Although the specific meanings of these three characters differ, they all serve to designate the very beginning of this teaching by means of the unsurpassed, secret,
and ultimate fruit— the fruit of that which is not a fruit.
△ Next, to indicate the breadth [of the subject]:
*Sūtra* is the general name for the sacred teachings; as for whether it has a translation or not, the matter is explained in detail below.
"The matter is explained in detail below" refers to the following four-line exposition, as well as the *Fahua Xuanyi*, fascicle eight.

Extensive Explanation. △ Next, regarding the section "If one possesses... and below, which provides a re-explanation, it is divided into three parts: first, the heading; second, the main explanation starting from "Furthermore, if...
and below; third, the summary starting from "In brief... and below, which distinguishes the three dharmas to correspond with the five chapters and marks the beginning of the Ultimate Teaching.
If one were to rely strictly upon the Sanskrit original, it should be called *mahā-parinirvāṇa*; here, it is translated as "Great Parinirvāṇa" (Dà mièdù).
The first part is according to the text.
△ Second, the formal explanation of the text itself is divided into three sections.
It is as vast as empty space, not dependent on small characteristics; furthermore, its nature is expansive and can contain much;
it is also called the inconceivable Dharma-realm of all Buddhas—these are the three meanings that explain "Great."
If "initially like empty space" refers to the ultimate emptiness of *prajñā*, and "its nature is below" refers to liberation (*vimukti*),
while "also named 'not below'" refers to the *dharmakāya*, then within each single name all three meanings are fully present.
△ Next, regarding "extinction" (*nirodha*).
"Extinction" means the extinction of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) and all false and deceptive things;

furthermore, it refers to attaining the twenty-five kinds of samādhi and manifesting various forms, as well as the principle that once birth and extinction have been extinguished, quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*) is bliss. These are the three meanings that explain "extinction."

The initial statement regarding the extinction of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). That which is empty and void is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), yet it is also the real dharma (*dharma-tattva*).

When both the internal and external, as well as the provisional and the real, are all forgotten, this is called ultimate emptiness. Furthermore, one attains the lower liberation; moreover, one extinguishes the arising of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Once arising and ceasing have been extinguished, this is the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth) of *nirvāṇa*. One forgets even the bliss of quiescent extinction.
Thus, even the substance of the Middle Way and Nirvana—the fundamental Dharma-realm—is unattainable.
△ Third, regarding the "crossing over":
crossing over means crossing over that which is not crossed, crossing over that which is crossed, and crossing over both this shore and the other shore; yet it is also non-crossing.
That which is not "this shore" is the "other shore"; it is like a divine tortoise that crosses both water and land—these are the three meanings that explain "crossing.

First is the principle (*dharma*), followed by the analogy. Within the principle, it says: "to cross over that which cannot be crossed" refers to *prajñā* (wisdom), [which delivers one] from the three delusions and two deaths.

Those who have not yet been delivered are all delivered; furthermore, they are delivered in the lower realm, which is liberation. Entering emptiness and emerging from the provisional, they are all established within the Dharma of liberation.
Moreover, they are delivered in this and that—the lower [level] is the *dharmakāya*. Birth-and-death is "this," and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is "that";
because the essence of the Middle Way is manifest, it spontaneously transcends both illumination and non-illumination. Therefore, it is said, "they are also delivered," and so forth.
△ Regarding the three pairs and five chapters:
encompassing the three dharmas, the three eyes, and the three points, it is named the Great Parinirvāṇa,
the Adamantine Treasure Store, complete and without deficiency, neither vertical nor horizontal, neither parallel nor distinct— this subtle and secret essence is eternally abiding.

Taking "transformation," "perpetual peace," "coolness," "agelessness," and "immortality" as its core tenet; placing poison within the Buddha-nature so that it permeates the five flavors, killing people with every taste;
and sounding the great drum of virulent poison such that all who hear it die—even without intending to—these constitute its function.
The two characters "Ever-abiding" (changzhu) are the unsurpassed clarified butter (amṛta), which distinguishes this work from all other scriptures.

The roar of meditative concentration (samādhi) corresponds to the name of the teaching; its essence encompasses the constant principle, and its function represents the ultimate characteristic of the teaching.

First, regarding the explanation of the name: "Vajra" (the diamond-like) and below, regarding the essence, both can be understood. Within the section on the principle (*tattva*), it says: "Constant" is the virtue of permanence (*nitya-guṇa*);

"ever-abiding" is the virtue of bliss (*sukha-guṇa*); "cooling" is the virtue of purity (*śubha-guṇa*); and "not aging," etc., are the virtue of self (*ātma-guṇa*). This applies to both the beginning and the end.

By constantly contemplating the four virtues, one observes the fruit arising from its own cause; thus it is said that [the teaching] accords with its fundamental principle and function, as can be understood.
Regarding the characteristics of the ultimate teaching: if it were not the perfect, eternal ultimate teaching, there would be no such "poisonous" function.

If the fundamental principle were not the eternal substance, it would not universally encompass all phenomena; how then could the name contain the secret treasury of the three virtues? This is clearly explained in the *Shi* (Commentary).

This sutra is briefly divided into six sections: first, clarifying the intent of the teaching; second, clarifying the primary purpose of the sutra; third, clarifying its essential nature; fourth, explaining the era of the teaching;

fifth, explaining the title of the sutra; and sixth, explaining the text of the sutra. The first section is divided into two parts. First, a general clarification of the intent of the teaching. Master Bao states:
"Among all the sutras, it is taught that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to the aspiration [for enlightenment]."
The vows and practices are all intended to cause all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood;
this sutra is likewise so, for it teaches that all bodhisattvas believe that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and shall attain Buddhahood.
The two distinct explanations regarding the intent of the sutra and so forth are as detailed in the extensive commentary and are not recorded here in full.
△ Next, regarding the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), we shall open the chapters to explain the text in detail. This is divided into two parts: first, the headings and enumeration;
second, the detailed exposition. The *Xuanyi* is opened into five layers:
1. Explanation of Names (*shiming*); 2. Explanation of Substance (*shiti*); 3. Explanation of the Thesis (*shizong*); 4. Explanation of Function (*shiyong*); 5. Explanation of Teaching (*shijiao*).

△ Next, the explanation within this major section is divided into chapters. First, the text explaining the names is divided into two parts: first, the presentation and enumeration; second, the actual explanation of the names.
This explanation of the names further consists of five categories: namely, the translated, the pervasive, the non-artificial, and the absolute.
△ Second, the explanation, which is further divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the summary.

The latter concludes by returning to the teaching of the four gates that transcends words. First, the formal explanation, which itself consists of five sections. First, the translation of the title, which is further divided into two:
first, clarifying the direct translation; second, explaining its meaning. The latter explains the meaning of the title. The first [section] is further divided into two, the first of which is...
The headings are listed as follows;
the translations consist of four propositions: namely, non-existence, existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.

△ Next, from the first phrase "below," the explanation is divided into three parts: first, showing the differences in the weight [of translation] across the five regions of India; second, like... [text continues].
The first part, "What is said below," correctly distinguishes the three different characteristics; the second part, "Each of them below," recounts the old [traditions].

Regarding the first point, as for the term "non-existent" (*amūla*), there are five different locations in India: the three regions of the east, south, and center differ slightly from one another, while the two regions of the northwest differ greatly.
The first part is as stated in the text.
△ Second, regarding the differences, there are three sections: first, describing those types; second, "Next, there is someone... and below, refuting erroneous views; third, "The *Vibhāṣā*...
and below, citing evidence to reveal the correct meaning.
For instance, when one says *mahā-mahī-nirvṛti*, this refers to three syllables; when one says *nirvāṇa*, this refers to two syllables.
These are merely like the regional variations between the dialects of Chu and Xia here in China.
The first part is as stated in the text.
△ Next, regarding the error concerning the "bank" (āna):

some take the term *ni-ri* (泥日) to refer to the two-fascicle *Nirvāṇa*, and take the term *ni-uan* (泥洹) to refer to the six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa*, and take the term *da-ben* (大本) to refer to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. This is their interpretation.
In all cases, this is not so. The two-fascicle version clarifies the eighty aspects of impermanence, while the six-fascicle version clarifies the indestructibility of the vajra;

how then can one simplify the meaning through local dialects? As for the phrase "how can one [simplify]... to the meaning": when translating names according to their meaning, how can local dialects possibly determine it?
△ Third, citing the *Vibhāṣā*: The *Vibhāṣā* states that it is *nirvāṇa*;

1. Regarding the five [aspects], the initial direct answer requires a comprehensive explanation because it relies upon the four *siddhi* (purposes/conditions).

As for seeking them as a combination within the three qualities, this is because a single quality is itself the three qualities.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "If a person perceives *prajñā*, they are bound; if they do not perceive *prajñā*, they are likewise freed from bondage.
If a person perceives *prajñā*, they attain liberation; if they do not perceive *prajñā*, they likewise attain liberation.
The liberation of the *dharmakāya* is also like this. It is, for example, like a magically conjured object which cannot be seen, yet..."
To see that which sees yet cannot be seen—this matter is rare and extraordinary.
This sutra is named "Subtle, Wondrous, and Inconceivable," and these three bodies are merely designated by the provisional name "Secret Treasury.
Nirvāṇa is merely designated by the provisional name; these three types of prajñā are [designated] as the "Three Eyes of Maheśvara" in nirvāṇa.

It is merely a provisional designation that the three gates of liberation are called the "three dots" of nirvāṇa; it is merely a provisional designation that the fulfillment of these three dharmas is called "Mahāparinirvāṇa.
It is merely a provisional designation used to guide sentient beings, just as an empty fist is used to delight small children and entice them.
To stop the crying of a child, one teaches a clever child; once the task is accomplished, one withdraws the pointing finger and opens the clenched fist—the fist is then no longer a fist.
Nirvāṇa is likewise: it is gladdened by the syllable *ni*, introduced by the syllable *ni*, destroyed by the syllable *ni*, and realized through the syllable *ni*.
These are the four kinds of benefits of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Once these benefits have been obtained, why should one still cling?
Does dispute arise from names?

Just as it is with the provisional designation of "existence," so too it is with the provisional designation of "non-existence," the provisional designation of "both existence and non-existence," and the provisional designation of "neither existence nor non-existence" (and so forth).
△ Regarding the eighth point on the intention of the compilation:
one should explain that it is about to cross over the causes and conditions (as explained at length). Furthermore, it is like the method for treating a choking person (as explained at length).

One should know that within these respective sections, the opening of provisional means (*upāya*) is nothing other than a nominal cause and condition for attracting sentient beings; the true reality is as follows.
The method for treating dysphagia is merely a form of mental visualization.

△ Fifth, the explanation of the term "severance" is divided into two parts: first, the formal exposition; second, the subsequent analysis using the phrase "now, below. The first part further contains two sections: first, recounting the interpretations of others;
second, refuting partiality by means of the teachings, beginning with the phrase "taking this... and so forth.
Regarding the fifth interpretation, "the severance of names": some explain "severance" as the extinction of existence and the preservation of non-existence;
however, if there is non-existence, it is not severed, and this is not what is intended here. Some explain "severance" as detachment, saying that within *nirvāṇa* there are no various existents;
yet even this is not the meaning of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), nor is it what is employed here. Some explain "severance" as cessation, saying it is the cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
To claim that "all things are non-existent" while still persisting in nirvāṇa like an extinguished fire is called a false interpretation and a fallacious objection in the sutras;
how could such a view be acceptable? Some cite a sutra which says: "It is like a great fragrant elephant that suddenly breaks its fetters and goes wherever it pleases."
The initial statement, "There are no various existences," means that there is neither the cause nor the fruit of the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
△ The subsequent passage also has two parts: first, it negates partiality;

second, it uses this to explain "the absolute" (*jue*). This refers to the meaning of one side of what is transcended by the Bodhisattva, as praised by the bhikṣu who practices the three types of cultivation.
The "not yet perfected" [state] is the same as the aforementioned meaning of "namelessness," which does not mean that names are now utterly severed.

△ Next, regarding the passage beginning with "If one says," it uses the teachings to demonstrate the severance and pervasiveness; herein there are four teachings. First, within the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching, there are four points:
first, it is not a state of non-opposition, nor is it the ultimate severance; next, from "If one knows the mind" onwards, it clarifies the stage of the worthy (*bhadra*).

Cultivating the severance of the three [delusions], if one enters the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it clarifies the holy stages where the four types of severance arise. This section below concludes the intent of severance:

if speech pursues its objects in succession—responding to non-existence by speaking of existence, or responding to existence by speaking of neither-existence-nor-non-existence—and if such waiting for and responding to objects does not cease, then words will never be severed.
If one discriminates with the mind, even a slight movement of thought or the arising of a mental conception, [the cycle continues].
If deluded thought itself does not cease, and since the mind does not cease, how can speech cease?
The initial statement that "the arising of thought in the mind is delusion" means that when the mind has thought, it is delusion, whereas without thought, it is nirvana.
That "the mind also does not cease" is because the mind is the cause of thought.

If one knows that the mind is the攀緣 (pān-yuan, object-conditioning) of the triple world, and that this object-conditioning of the triple world—which arises and ceases—is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, then by ceasing this object-conditioning mind, there is no mind to be attained. Because the mind is cut off, its expressions are also cut off.
This is what is meant by "the path of speech is severed and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished" through cultivation; it is not a true cessation.

If one enters the patience regarding the realization of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the light of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) dawns; at the moment of death, this is termed "birth" yet "non-birth. Śāriputra said:
"I have heard that within liberation there is no verbal expression, and that within liberation there is no conceptual discrimination.
This is true realization wherein the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases; it is the cessation of all intentional thought within the Tripiṭaka.
△ Regarding the fourth section on the summary of the intent:
it points out that this single [teaching] transcends how many persons and dharmas, let alone others.
As for "transcending how many persons and dharmas," it refers to the three schools, the six schools, and the heterodoxies of both the internal and external vehicles of the Hīnayāna.
For ordinary people in the stage of mundane rank, one should teach the Dharma of the four gates as well as the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas;

when all these are utterly transcended, there is nothing that is not fully understood regarding the true reality of persons, let alone other heterodox views—how much more so the transcendence of the common and the particular, which was not even known by the ancients.
△ Now, following the entry into Truth, the next section clarifies the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), which is divided into two parts. First, it refutes the constraints of the Tripitaka (Zang).

When entering Truth, the transcendence of contemplation is severed; why is it not severed? Because Truth and the conventional are distinct; thus, one is severed while the other is not, and their mutual dependence remains manifest. How, then, can this be called "severance"?

△ Next, regarding the thorough explanation that can penetrate downward, there are two parts: first, clarifying the severance practiced in the stage of the *śaikṣa* (the Worthy); second, from "If it is empty...
onwards, clarifying the severance manifested in the stage of the *aśaikṣa* (the Sage).
If one can [realize this], how distant is the Way? It is the truth within phenomena themselves. How distant is the Sage? Its essence is the very spirit. When seeing form...
It is like the sound heard by the blind, or like an echo; for that which expounds the Dharma, there is neither speaking nor showing.

For that which discriminates, there is nothing to be discriminated. It is neither severed nor unsevered, yet it is called "severed. This, too, is the path of skillful means wherein the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
The initial statement, "How sublime and distant it is! means that the Way is not distant; by contemplating the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one realizes they are the Truth (*tattva*).
Thus, "to embody it is to be spiritual" means to penetrate the mind as being identical to Principle (*li*).

If one accords with the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) and enters the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), there is a sudden, vast purity—nothing can be severed, and there is nothing to be severed.
"Exhaustion is the absence of a dharma of exhaustion"—this is the meaning of the term "exhaustion" (jue) in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

△ Although this [Shared Teaching] darkly aligns with the three insights of the lower [vehicles], the Separate Teaching (Biejiao) is divided into two parts: first, it refutes that which is shared by the Shared Teaching as not being distant;
second, it provides the formal explanation.
Although this [state] darkens the True, it has not yet darkened the Middle; although it severs the pervasive, it has not yet severed the specific. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"If the fetters and habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted, flowers will cling to the body. Furthermore, the text below states: "As long as ignorance has not been expelled, it causes the sun and moon to revolve, like one suffering from malaria.

This refers to the fact that while the delusions regarding the external realms are severed in relation to those within the realm, the conceptual delusions regarding the pervasive remain unsevered in relation to the specific delusions. Thus, they are not yet cut off.

The initial statement, "like one suffering from malaria," means that just as malaria occurs on one day and not on another, so too have the pervasive afflictions (*pariyutthāna*) been severed while the specific afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have not yet been severed; thus, it is compared to malaria.
△ Next, in the main exposition, there are two parts. First, regarding the stage of the former sages and the cultivation of cessation:
if one can cultivate the five practices with a mind of Great Nirvana and possess the ten merits, at that time one will single-mindedly and exclusively seek the practice of Great Nirvana;
there will no longer be a mind directed toward the realms within [the triple world], nor will there be any discourse concerning the realms within. It is only in this way that—
This is also termed "the severance of the path of speech and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity," yet it is not yet [the state of] profound darkness.
△ Next, if one awakens to the lower noble stage, one realizes the ultimate;
if one awakens to the Middle Way, the merit attained is not shared with Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, being that which was previously unattained.
Now that this has been attained, what was previously not severed is now severed; this is likely the meaning of the term "severance" (jue) in the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

Furthermore, from the point after this, when one cultivates the Middle Way, enters the stages (bhūmi), and realizes the Middle, it should also be said that this is "not shared with the six [vehicles] such as the śrāvakas," and likewise "not shared with the bodhisattvas of the provisional means (upāya)."
△ However, regarding the realization of the "extinction of the lower" (jue-xia) and the "perfect extinction" (yuan-jue), these two are also first critiqued as distinct and then correctly explained.

At the time of realizing extinction, one is indeed identical to the ultimate perfection (yuan-ji); yet during the stage of cultivation, the rungs of the ladder and the flow of the river are winding and circuitous. Why is this?

Because the arousal of the mind cannot pervade the entire Dharma-realm, and because there remains something further outside the Dharma-realm; thus it is not called the "extinction of phenomena" (jue-fa), for it is clumsy.
To practice that which cannot be practiced is the practice of the Tathāgata; because there is further practice beyond the practice of the Tathāgata, it is not called the "termination of practice.
It is not that there is no supreme skillful means; rather, because there are further skillful means beyond skillful means, it is not the "termination of skillful means."

The initial statement regarding the winding of rivers and streams means that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) comes first, followed by the provisional (*prajñapti*), and then the middle (*madhyama*); it is thus.

As for the existence of dharmas outside the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), this is because within the middle there exist the three truths of emptiness, the provisional, and their perfect fusion (*yuanrong*).

△ Next, in the main exposition, there are three parts: first, clarifying the stages of the sages; second, [addressing] the objection that the opening of the lower sage-stages contradicts the realization of the ultimate [in the third stage];
and third, citing various sutras to establish consistency. Regarding the first, there are two further sections: first, clarifying how the three teachings and four gates open into the Perfect;
second, clarifying how the four gates of the Perfect transcend contemplation. Regarding the first of these, there are five sub-sections; the first cites a sutra to establish [the position].

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): if one fully arouses the mind to contemplate Great Nirvāṇa, all mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Beyond this Dharma-realm, there is no further Dharma-realm;

because it is the solitary, unique Dharma-realm, it is called the "transcendent Dharma-realm" (*atyanta-dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, as a sūtra states: "Moreover, there is one practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata."
Because there is no further practice beyond that of the Tathāgata, it is called the "uniquely transcendent practice. Furthermore, as the sutra says:
"Directly abandoning expedient means, he teaches only the Unsurpassed Way. Just as the continent of Nikūya enters directly into the western ocean like a straight line, so too is this transcendent.
Skillful Means.
△ Next, regarding "severing skillful means" and below, this opens the storehouse to enter reality.
"Severing skillful means" means that, as the sutra says, because one has severed all nets of doubt within the mind, it is called liberation. 3.
The four gates of the treasury are themselves the Dharma-realm, themselves the practice of the Tathāgata, and themselves the supreme skillful means.
Since birth and death are themselves nirvāṇa, how much more so for the Śrāvaka-dharma, which gives rise to a mind of certainty—how could one ever give rise to a web of doubt?
△ 3. The "Common" (tōng) below opens into the Real:
because the four gates of the Common Teaching (tōngjiào) are likewise the Dharma-realm, and the net of doubts regarding the shared vehicle (gòngshèng) is severed.
△ 4. The "Distinct" (bié) below opens into the Distinct.
The four gates of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) are precisely the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); because the net of doubts regarding the Bodhisattva vehicle is severed.
△ Fifth, this clarifies the concluding intent below:
This is called the mind that severs all nets of doubt; it is named "Solitary and Absolute Liberation" (*ekānta-vimukti*), teaching only the single Dharma-realm.
It is not said that one should contemplate only the single dharma-realm while not contemplating other dharma-realms;
this is what is meant by the severance of the path of language and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity within the path of skillful means.

△ Next, within the section on the four gates of perfection, there are likewise four gates of perfect skillful means. If one says that all phenomena are transcended and there is only the single Dharma-realm, this refers to the gate of existence, wherein even the name "transcendence" is absent.
If one says that within the Dharma-realm there is not even a Dharma-realm, how much less could there be anything else?

This refers to the negation of names through the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If one says that the subtle and wondrous Dharma-realm is such that one dharma is the three dharmas and the three dharmas are one dharma, this refers to the negation of names through the gate of both existence and non-existence.

If one says that the Dharma-realm is inconceivable, this refers to the negation of names through the gate of neither existence nor non-existence. All of these are the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*).
To say that one dharma is three dharmas means that while the three dharmas appear distinct, their names are likewise identical within the single substance of the Dharma-realm;
there is no longer even the name of "three.
If one speaks of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, it is like using a golden probe to remove the film from the eye: with two fingers or three fingers, [the vision] becomes perfectly clear.
It is clear that this is called the ultimate transcendence of words: words fill the Dharma-realm yet there is not a single word;
the mind fills the Dharma-realm yet there is not a single thought. This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching’s transcendence of names.
△ Third, citing similar passages, part four first cites the *Mahāvaipulya* to prove the ultimate [emptiness].

However, although various sūtras speak of the "ultimate," their underlying meanings are not uniform. The *Avataṃsaka* says: "It is like grasping at empty space or wind; it is like painting within empty space.
Having already stated that this is difficult even to explain, how much more so to demonstrate it to others? The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says: "All dharmas do not depend upon one another."
Because not a single thought abides for even a moment; furthermore, while various bodhisattvas speak, Mañjuśrī speaks of non-speaking, and Vimalakīrti remains silent, cutting off all speech.
Next, from the section on Subhūti onwards, he cites the arguments of the lesser sages and bodhisattvas to prove the cessation of speech.
Śubhūti said: "I have nothing to say; I neither perceive nor attain [it]. Nāgārjuna said: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon in turn establishes its dependence.
Now, there being no cause for dependence, there is likewise no phenomenon to be established."
Now, there is no cause by which one could attain the "lower"; this phrase is used precisely to prove absolute non-existence.
△ Third, from "The present sutra" onwards, it clarifies the greatness of the present sutra’s transcendence of all dependencies.
The present sutra says: "For example, space is not called 'great' because of a small space; Nirvana is likewise."
It is because of these minor characteristics that it is called Great Nirvana. Why are they called minor characteristics?

Everything from what is realized by the followers of the Two Vehicles up to the peace and bliss within saṃsāra are all minor characteristics; it is not because of these minor things that it is named "Great. Furthermore, it is said:
"For example, if there is a dharma that cannot be measured and is inconceivable, it is then called Great Nirvana. It is likewise immeasurable.
Because it is inconceivable, it is called "Great.
△ Fourth, from "One should know" onwards, the conclusion of the correct [teaching] follows.
One should know that the meaning of Nirvana beyond names is now manifest. Although these texts are numerous and their adaptations to various conditions differ, they cannot... [be fully enumerated].
A general summary.

△ Next, regarding the "Discernment" (Liao Jian), there are three parts: first, the headings and enumeration; second, the explanation beginning with "How is it..."; third, the re-explanation of "extinction" beginning with "How is it the extinction of extinction...".
Now, I shall analyze this by means of four propositions: non-interruption, interruption, neither non-interruption nor interruption, and double interruption.

What is "non-interruption"? It is as in the case of the six realms of existence, the blissful states, and so forth. What is "interruption"? It is as in the case of the Tripiṭaka and the Shared [Vehicle], and so forth.
What is "neither non-interruption nor interruption"? It is as in the case of citing the four gates, and so forth. What is "double interruption"? It refers to the four gates of the Perfect [Teaching].
This is so. The first two [sections] are as stated in the text.
△ Regarding the third section, the "Threefold Explanation":

What is meant by "extinguishing the extinguisher"? Because it can extinguish that which is to be extinguished, it is called "extinguishing the extinguisher. From the four gates of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha) downward, these are termed "that which is to be extinguished";

from the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (Bodhisattva), they are termed "the extinguisher. By means of the extinguisher, that which is to be extinguished is extinguished, and the extinguisher itself is also extinguished.
It is like the fire and wood: once the wood has burned the grass, the fire itself is naturally extinguished. One should know that the name "extinguishing" is identical to "non-existence."
The meaning of "difference" (viśeṣa) lies herein; therefore, it is said that "even cessation is ceased.

As for the statement "that which can cease is also ceased": what is currently being ceased is the cessation itself, which is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). How could there be anything further capable of ceasing it?

Hence it is said, "that which can cease is also ceased. Furthermore, regarding "it is also naturally so": beginning from the stage of contemplative practice (vipaśyanā-caryā), fire and wood are [already] such.
To be the same as grasses and trees is called the severance of contemplative practice (guanxing).
△ Next, [the section] is divided into five parts: first, the presentation of the fivefold meaning;
second, the summary and explanation of the names. This single chapter is opened into five layers, all of which embody the intent of the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
△ Next, from "If the Great Nirvāṇa" onwards is the formal explanation.
If the Great Nirvāṇa is called "True, Good, and Sublime Existence," it has existed inherently from the beginning and is not something that has merely come into being now;

this is because it follows the meaning of the "Gate of Existence" (yǒumén), and thus its name is translated and explained through the same term. If the Great Nirvāṇa is [understood as] emptiness, it is like the emptiness of the city of Kapilavastu.
Because this is the meaning of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is explained by means of the "nameless" (*anāmakam*);
if the Great Nirvāṇa is both form and non-form, this is the meaning of the gate of both emptiness and existence, and thus it is explained by means of "provisional names" (*prajñapti-nāman*);

if the Great Nirvāṇa is called the Middle Way because it excludes the two extremes, this is the meaning of the gate of neither emptiness nor existence, and thus it is explained by means of the "transcendent name" (*atyantānāmakam*).
△ Third, the section below "The Great Nirvāṇa" distinguishes its various names.
Now, the Great Nirvāṇa is not even a single entity; how then could it be four? These "four" refer to its gates.
Gates are established to indicate principles and thus possess manifold names. Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has a thousand names, so too does liberation have many names.
[This concludes the section on] Names. △ Fourth, citing evidence from below the section on Names:
The "Chapter on the Merits of Names" states, "Nirvāṇa is the name; all other praises and eulogies are its designations."
△ Fifth: "If that is so," and below, the interrogation and explanation.
If that is so, *nirvāṇa* is the totality, yet for the sake of those suited to the teaching (*yathābhavyatā*), it is established as a name;
the three dots (*bindu*) and all other elements belong to the syllables (*akṣara*). If the *dharmakāya* is the totality for those suited to the teaching, it is further named *nirvāṇa* and all else.

When things have already returned to their names, if they were thus subject to mutual indeterminacy, even though they are indeterminate, now that they are definitively designated by the name "Nirvāṇa," whether determinate or indeterminate, general or particular, all are devoid of relative counterparts;
they are entirely inconceivable and entirely transcendent. Therefore, it is called the Great Transcendent Nirvāṇa.

All is as stated in the text. △ The second major section, "Explaining the Substance," is divided into two parts: first, a summary of previous interpretations; second, "Now, to clarify... which constitutes the formal explanation.

This first part has three sections: first, an explanation based on the Two Truths; second, "Since ancient times... which explains it based on the Three Sages; third, "Furthermore, since ancient times... [which continues the discussion].

The following section explains [the nature of nirvāṇa] by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This part consists of two sections: first, a presentation of the four schools of thought; second, the critique beginning with "There is another person who...

The second section explains the essence of nirvāṇa. First, it presents the old interpretation: the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Zhuangyan) states that the nirvāṇa of the Buddha-fruit lies outside the two truths and is not subsumed under either the ultimate (*paramārtha*) or the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Ordinary beings, through the cause of delusion, produce results; these are the floating and empty conventional truth, which is a provisional entity.
Because it is empty, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); because the fruit of Buddhahood is not produced by the causes of delusion, it is not the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

and because it cannot be further emptied, it is not the ultimate truth. As the *Renyō-kyō* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra) states: "Transcending both the conventional truth and the ultimate truth, one dwells in the eleventh stage, the stage of *sarvajñā*.
Kaigen (Kaisan) says that the nirvana of the fruit of Buddhahood is still subsumed within the two truths as its essence.

Because this continuity depends upon two kinds of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); because these two conventions can themselves be emptied, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The numinous wisdom of the Buddha-fruit likewise merges with the ultimate. Yecheng Xi said: "The nirvana of the Buddha-fruit is not the conventional truth; it is the ultimate truth.
Because it is subtle, wondrous, quiescent, and absolute, it is said that at the time of death according to conventional truth, it is called 'birth' and 'non-birth. Longguang said: "The Buddha..."

The fruition of nirvāṇa possesses both the provisional designations of continuity (*prabandha-prajñapti*) and mutual dependence (*apekṣā-prajñapti*); as such, it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is the sense of "immediacy with the Real" (*ji-ji zhen*).

Yet, this is not a state of being merged with the Real; for if one were merged with the Real, one would be identical to an insentient object, which is the wisdom of cloudless [emptiness] and therefore not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

First, regarding the fourfold initial adornment, there are two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of evidence from the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) and below, as in the text.

The remaining two masters can both be understood. Within the section on Longguang (Nāgārjuna), it says that "stubborn objects" (*wanjian*) refer to the biased emptiness of the Two Vehicles, which is termed a "stubborn object."
△ Next, regarding the refutation, there are four parts: first, the formal refutation and critique; second, the citation of scriptural evidence as stated in the *Lun yun* (The Treatise says) below;

third, the judgment that this belongs to non-Buddhist views rather than being the true Nirvana, as indicated by "Zhaoyi" below; and fourth, the proof that it is a mistaken adherence, as stated in the *Jing yun* (The Sutra says) below.

Why, then, do you claim in your own system that the Buddha-fruit is exclusively unconditioned? On the other hand, if the Buddha-fruit is subsumed within the two truths, it should be both conditioned and unconditioned.
Furthermore, if the Buddha-fruit is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the ultimate truth cannot..."

To say that there is no utility for sentient beings while asserting that the Buddha-fruit exists as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and further claiming that the Buddha-fruit is invariably existent—these are all assertions by the masters of the Chengshi (Satyasiddhi) school that contradict their own fundamental tenets; they neither satisfy human sentiment nor accord with the *Zhao lun*.
First, regarding the statement that "it does not satisfy human sentiment at all," if it fails to satisfy even the sentiments of ordinary people, how can it be called a discourse on the Sage’s Dharma?
△ Second, falling into the fallacy of negation.
The treatise says: It cannot be grasped through form or name, nor can it be known through the mind. To speak of it is to lose its truth; to know it is to fall back into folly.
To affirm its existence is to deviate from its nature; to deny its existence is to harm the person.
To say that "knowing" reverses one's folly is merely to say that it results in further folly.

Master Zhao’s intention in examining this is that [such a view] falls into the four views and lies outside the realm of the Buddha-dharma; it is not even the gate of the Lesser Nirvāṇa, let alone the essence of the Lesser Nirvāṇa.
Since it is not even the essence of the gate of the Lesser Nirvāṇa, how could it possibly be the essence of the gates of the Common or Distinct Nirvāṇas?
If it is neither the common nor the distinct gate, how can its essence be the essence of the Great Nirvāṇa?
The Sūtra says: "These people, during the month of spring, went out in boats for recreation and lost a lapis lazuli gem.

△ Next, within the Guangzhai [school]:
Guangzhai says that the eternally abiding Buddha-fruit has two kinds of neutral (avyākṛta) states: first, the neutral of understanding and realization; second, the neutral of karmic retribution.
Because it exists even in icchantikas, it is not wholesome; because it also exists in the stage of Buddhahood, it is not unwholesome. Thus, it is of a neutral nature.
As for "karmic retribution," it is like the suffering of birth and death; since the retribution is impermanent, [it is neutral].
It is neither evil, but rather indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); even the state of nirvāṇa—characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity—is not virtuous, but is simply indeterminate.
