Regarding the first, the four truths of arising and ceasing:

the accumulation (samudaya) is that which gives rise [to suffering], and suffering is that which is given rise to. That which gives rise is the giver of rise, and that which is given rise to is the object of rise.

That which arises again is the origin that gives rise to suffering; the revolving cycle of birth and death has no end. The Path is called that which can destroy, while these [other truths] are what is destroyed.

That which is destroyed destroys that which destroys it, and that which destroys it is also destroyed by that which is destroyed; because they arise and perish in mutual relation, they are called the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing.
The first passage states that the Path is called "that which can destroy" because the Path possesses the power to destroy Suffering and its Origin;

since Cessation is named after the place where Suffering and its Origin are extinguished, it is said that Cessation is "that which is destroyed. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "mutually arising and ceasing":

when Suffering and its Origin exist, the Path and Cessation do not exist; when the Path and Cessation exist, Suffering and its Origin do not exist; and likewise, when the Path exists [the others do not].
Because there is no path at the time when cessation exists, and because the path does not exist [at that time], it is said that they are "mutually [dependent].
△ Next, regarding the demonstration of their characteristics:
as for their characteristics, such as the pressing and the growth, and the ability to eliminate that which is to be eliminated, it is as stated in the Sūtra.

Oppression is the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*); arising and growth are the characteristic of origination (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*); that which can eliminate is the characteristic of the path (*mārga-lakṣaṇa*); and that which is eliminated is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
△ Second, regarding non-arising (*anutpāda*), there are two parts: first, the explanation; second, the demonstration of its characteristics.

Regarding the Four Truths of Non-arising: one investigates the root of suffering and its origin and finds that they are fundamentally non-arising. Because they do not arise, there is neither suffering nor its origin.
Since there is nothing to be destroyed, there is also nothing capable of destroying; thus they are called the Four Truths of Non-arising. To explain their characteristics:
one understands that suffering is without suffering, yet possesses the True Truth (*satya*); the same applies to the origin, the path, and cessation. As the Sūtra says: [omitted].

The first passage states that "one who can investigate suffering and its origin" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Next, within the section on demonstrating the characteristics, it says "one who understands suffering as being without suffering" refers to the Truth of the Path.
△ Third, the Immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Regarding the four truths of the three immeasurables: the analytical reckoning of the immeasurable characteristics of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, as stated in the sūtra.
△ Fourth, the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra).

Regarding the four truths as one reality: one understands that suffering is without suffering, yet there is reality; and so on, up to understanding that cessation is without cessation, yet there is reality.
This "reality" is neither suffering, nor the cause of suffering, nor the exhaustion of suffering, nor the antidote to suffering;
rather, it is the single reality. This applies likewise even to cessation. This is called the four truths as one reality, as fully described in the sutra.
All is as stated in the text.
△ Third, regarding the revelation [of the truth]:

it is not that there is a separate "one true" Four Noble Truths apart from the "arising and ceasing" Four Noble Truths; rather, one realizes that arising and ceasing themselves are the one true [truth].
The four truths, non-arising, and the immeasurables are likewise thus: within one there is the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable there is one;
it is inconceivable and cannot be shown or explained.

As for "within one there is the immeasurable," this is because the provisional exists within the real. As for "within the immeasurable there is one," this is because [the real exists] within the provisional.
Because it possesses reality, it is inconceivable; this means that it simultaneously negates both extremes and illuminates both extremes, which is why it is called "inconceivable" and so forth.
△ Fourth, regarding the five chapters:
Because it makes the conceptualization of intense desire easy to understand, the proclamation of the "one reality" and the four truths is its name.
Taking the single truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) constitutes its essence; thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that the "one reliance" is precisely the single truth of cessation.

The truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) corresponds to its primary principle, while taking that which is to be remedied by the truth of the path corresponds to its function. To harmonize and delight the mind, this reality is thus proclaimed.
The Truths (satya) are precisely what is called the Teaching; although they are explained with distinctions, they are but a single, undifferentiated Dharma.

Regarding the "one basis" (ekāśraya), "one" refers to that which is the basis. One who takes joy in the mind while preaching the True Truth (satyadharma) opens the gate to the True [Truth] of the Hīnayāna and enters the True [Truth] of Buddha-nature;
it is only when the mind rejoices that, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one is included within the revealed teachings (*vyākaraṇa*).
Because the Buddha’s intent was not yet fully expressed in that [previous] discourse, it does not constitute ultimate joy.
(One chapter is omitted herein).
The fourth chapter on "Non-arising" is missing; as it is explained extensively in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Chapter on the Virtuous King), it will not be discussed here.
△ Five sections concerning the correct nature (*samyaktva*): 1. Listing the sequence; 2. Correct explanation; 3. "One should know" and below, the integration; 4.
"Those with strong desire" and below, the correlation with the fifth chapter; 5. "If a person" and below, concluding the previous and introducing the subsequent.

Fifth, regarding the classification by way of the true nature (*bhūtatā*), there are five kinds of nature: namely, the nature of the cause of the true nature, the nature of the cause of that cause, the nature of the fruit, the nature of the fruit of that fruit, and [the nature of] the true nature itself.
The first is as stated in the text.
△ Next, in the explanation:
"Right nature" (samyaktva) means it is not a cause, nor a cause of causes; it is not a fruit, nor a fruit of fruits; this is called right nature.

"Causing nature" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination. "Causes-and-causes nature" refers to the wisdom produced by the twelve links of dependent origination. "Fruit nature" refers to the three [vehicles].
Regarding the nature of the fruit of the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is Mahāparinirvāṇa, let us now discuss it by way of a single matter:

the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the so-called "correct cause" (*samyak-hetu*) Buddha-nature; the contemplation of the five aggregates as being of the nature of the cause is the "cause of the cause" nature;
the increase and fulfillment of this wisdom is the "nature of the fruit"; and that which is extinguished by this wisdom is the "nature of the fruit of the fruit."
Since it is thus with the aggregates (*skandha*), so it is with all other phenomena as well.
To speak briefly by way of a single instance: setting aside the twelve links of dependent origination, let us consider the single phenomenon of the five aggregates.

As for the reason why the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is established within these five aggregates: it is simply because this very delusion regarding the aggregates possesses the essence of the Dharma-body of true nature at the stage of fruition.
Regarding the reason why the five aggregates (*skandha*) are the nature of causes within the section on "Names": it is because they are observed as the nature of causes;

since they arise from the nature of causes and constitute causes through that causal nature, they are termed "causes of causes. As for all other phenomena, this refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the dependent retributions—all of which are likewise so.
△ Regarding the third [section], the mutual integration:
one should know that the five natures are neither distinct nor separate; they are five within oneness and one within five.
Oneness does not confuse the five, and the five do not depart from oneness. This is inconceivable and cannot be fully expressed.
"Clouds" refers to the "one," which is simply the one *nirvāṇa*-buddha-nature of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).

△ Fourth, within the five chapters, because it is desired to provide a forced differentiation for the sake of easy understanding: the name is designated as the "fruition-of-fruition nature," and the essence is designated as the "correct nature."
Taking the nature of cause and the nature of effect as the thesis, and taking the nature of cause as the function, this fivefold differentiation of natures is established for the sake of teaching;
yet, although it is thus differentiated, it is but a single dharma, with no further distinction.
To designate the nature of the fruit as its name refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa, which is the title of this very sutra.

To designate the nature of the cause as its function means that by contemplating the aggregates (skandhas) as causes, one brings about the fruit; since the function of the aggregates within the fruit universally arises across the ten realms to lead beings into the reality [of Nirvāṇa], the nature of the cause is designated as the function of this sutra.

If one can understand it in this way, not only will the substance of consciousness be clear and cool regarding names, principles, functions, teachings, and encountered phenomena, but for those who have not yet understood, I shall further discuss the principle.
△ The third major section, "Explaining the Principle," is divided into three parts: first, a brief refutation of past views; second, "As for the principle... and below, the formal explanation.
Third, summarizing these [points] below in relation to the five chapters:
regarding the third section, which clarifies the tenet of *nirvāṇa*, some say that the essence of the tenet is not different [from its phenomena]; this interpretation is incorrect. Why?

If one discusses the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*), duality is non-duality and non-duality is duality—this would indeed be appropriate. However, if one discusses names and phenomena (*nāma-vastu*)...
The non-dual cannot be made dual, and the dual cannot be made non-dual; since the essence of the established thesis is thus fixed, how could it possibly be identical?

First, there are two parts: first, a brief refutation, and second, the explanation of the reason for this, beginning with "Why is this so? Within this, the phrase "this is indeed appropriate" means that it accords with the capacities of sentient beings;
the statement "it is called a phenomenon" refers to the fact that, although it pertains to the essence of the fruit, it is designated by name.
It is established through practice.

△ Second, the formal explanation of the text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation; second, the clarification of the essential tenet (*siddhānta*). Regarding the latter, there are two sections:
first, the statement of the intent for establishing the tenet.
The "Essential Principle" (zōng) refers to the core; regarding the practice of cultivation, nothing surpasses cause and effect as its vital gateway.

△ Next, from "Furthermore, this sutra... onwards is the formal explanation, which is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, from "Question: To clarify... onwards, the response given to manifest their commonality.

The first part [the formal explanation] is further divided into three: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the formal explanation; third, from "However, this... onwards, the conclusion that returns to the ultimate purport.
This sutra clarifies that there are briefly three kinds of causes.
The first is as stated in the text.

△ Second, the formal explanation of the text itself consists of three parts; the first clarifies the connection from the Perfect [Teaching] to the Shared [Teaching], which further has two parts, the first being the formal explanation.
Next, the questions and answers below resolve doubts. This section first has three parts: (1) citing scriptures to demonstrate the essential characteristics;

(2) explaining the reasons for the inferiority [of other teachings]; and (3) clarifying that the revelation and manifestation are beyond waiting for or relying upon persons or dharmas, being non-dual.
First, the refutation of the cultivation of permanence based on impermanence, as in the *Śoka-parivarta*:

by means of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, [the Buddha] rebuked the bhikṣus for their impermanence, suffering, non-self, and unreality, stating that these should be abandoned. Now, for your sake, I shall explain the three superior cultivations;
this is the refutation of the cultivation of permanence based on impermanence, which can attain the fruit of permanence and reveals the defilements that are neither permanent nor impermanent.
Taking wisdom as the fuel and [insight] as the fire, by these causes and conditions, the food of nirvāṇa is prepared, causing all disciples to relish it with delight.
This is as stated in the text at the beginning.
△ Next, in the explanation:
the three inferior cultivations are the fuel of afflictions; the three superior cultivations are the fire of wisdom; "neither permanent nor impermanent" is the food of nirvana;
and the fourfold assembly abiding within the secret treasury is the sweet relish.
Regarding the statement that "the fuel of afflictions" refers to the sands of *avidyā* (ignorance) as the fuel:

it is further stated that because it is the essence (*tattva*) of the Tathāgata, it is therefore eternal. This "essence" is the path; because the dharma practiced along this path is eternal, the Buddha is also eternal.
Furthermore, because this dharma is neither eternal nor non-eternal, the Buddha is likewise neither eternal nor non-eternal.
...and so forth.
△ Second, the resolution of doubts is divided into two parts: first, the question;

[the question is as follows: First, for Cunda, he spoke directly of one "permanence," and next he explained the two characters "eternal-abiding" (nitya-sthita), and subsequently he rebuked the bhikṣus.
Regarding the question of why the three superior cultivations vary in their increase and decrease:
first, the response provides the direct answer to refute the [opponent’s] intent; second, from "In the past it was said... onwards, it answers the reasons for the two [types of cultivation];
third, from "It is said that the bhikṣu... onwards, it answers how they accord with the capacities of the audience and are thus appropriate.
Answer: These are all matters of contrast between the ancient and the present. The ancients spoke of the four non-eternals as collectively constituting one impermanence;
the present discussion treats the four virtues as collectively constituting one permanence. By citing this collective permanence, one refutes that collective impermanence.
Previously, it was taught that birth and death are impermanent and further characterized by flux; now, permanence is used to refute birth and death, and stability is used to refute flux.
Thus, two characters are raised to refute these two [concepts].
The first two [points] are as stated in the text.
△ Third, regarding "attaining what is appropriate":

while the various bhikṣus set aside the facts and rely solely on reasoning to cultivate the three perceptions (*saṃjñā*), here we cite the superior principle to refute the inferior one and employ it alone.
Regarding the "three cultivations" (and so forth):

as for setting aside the matter, this clarifies that contemplating the impurity of the body is the specific practice; however, because it is appropriate to follow the conditions of one's particular circumstances, it is set aside for the time being.
△ Second, regarding the passage on entering Great Nirvana suddenly rather than gradually, it is divided into four parts: first, establishing the practice to form the cause;

second, cultivating this [practice] below to clarify the realization of the fruit once the cause is formed; third, "One should know" below, which provides the concluding judgment; and fourth, "The King of Virtues" below, which cites scriptural evidence.
Within the first section, establishing the practice:

Second, with the mind of Great Nirvana, one cultivates the gradual training from the shallow to the deep, as in the Holy Practices (*ārya-caryā*), where one specifically practices the five types of conduct.
First is the precept; concentration and wisdom follow. Dwelling at home is like a prison, while the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) is like empty space.
From head to foot, one observes that within it there is only hair, fur, nails, teeth, large and small intestines, and the stomach—contemplating the eight sufferings and the five [aggregates].

The flourishing aggregates and so forth are next explained as being neither suffering nor non-suffering, yet possessing a true reality; subsequently, the immeasurable and boundless discrimination and calculation of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are [likewise explained];
finally, that which is neither suffering, nor its origin, nor the path, nor its cessation possesses a real truth—this is explained at length as in the sutra.

The precepts for householders and others constitute the practice of the lower [stages]; from the beginning down to the end, they constitute the practice of the lower [stages]. Observing these constitutes the practice of wisdom.
△ Next, regarding the realization of the fruit:
having cultivated these practices, one attains the twenty-five samādhis and abides in Great Nirvāṇa; how much more so will one manifest the merits of all Buddhas?
It can no longer be described.
One who has already cultivated these practices is said to have "already" entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
It should be understood that from the shallow to the deep, causes are formed and fruits are realized; yet, from beginning to end, there is nothing that is not both non-cause and non-fruit.
This is the constant principle.
△ Fourth, regarding the citation of evidence, there are two parts.
In the "Chapter on King Virtue," it is likewise stated: first, contemplate the four great elements as a chest, the five aggregates as a murderer, and the six sense objects as...
Craving is like an enemy; the afflictions are like a river; the eightfold path is like a raft. By moving the hands and feet, one cuts through the current and reaches the other shore.
Precept and concentration are like moving the feet; wisdom is like moving the hands; nirvana is that other shore.
It is also thus within the Lion’s Roar: beginning from few desires and contentment, it culminates in abiding in great nirvana. Furthermore:

To skillfully cultivate the precepts without perceiving the cause of the precepts, the fruit of the precepts, or the oneness and twoness of the precepts—this is called skillfully cultivating concentration and wisdom;
it is likewise for all else. From beginning to end, all take the eternally abiding as their fundamental principle; thus it is clear that the eternally abiding is taken as the fundamental principle.
The initial individual realization of King Virtue (*Guṇarāja*) and the subsequent individual realization of Lion’s Roar (*Siṃhanāda*) may both be seen [in the text].
△ Third, clarifying the meaning of the unique perfection:
Third, as it says in the "Noble Practices" (*Āryacaryā*): "Furthermore, there is one practice that is the practice of the Tathāgata, namely, the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*)."
The Mahāyāna of parinirvāṇa is precisely the cultivation of the cause, and parinirvāṇa is the attainment of the fruit. What is there that this Mahāyāna as a cause cannot transport?
What is there that the fruit of Great Nirvāṇa cannot achieve? For all beings without exception, there is no single path for transcending birth and death that surpasses this.
This general outline is sufficient to understand; it need not be explained in further detail.
As in the text.

△ Third, the conclusion and dedication, which also has two parts: first, the conclusion indicating the limits of the revelation; second, from "although there are three" onwards, the conclusion and dedication to the doctrine of permanence. Regarding the first part:

However, throughout this text, the various discussions regarding the practice or cultivation of the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*), the knowledge of faculties (*indriya*), and the knowledge of inclinations (*chanda*) differ in their particulars;

yet they do not transcend three types. First, by refuting impermanence (*anitya*) to cultivate permanence (*nitya*), one employs the principle of the Perfect [Teaching] to connect with the Small [Vehicle], and the Connecting [Teaching] to connect with the Small [Vehicle].
Second, one cultivates impermanence with the mind of Great Nirvāṇa. Third, one subsequently cultivates permanence; these constitute entry from the gradual [teaching].
"Sudden" and "gradual" refer to distinct intentions. To subsequently cultivate the permanent within the impermanent is the person of the Perfect-Sudden [teaching].
As for the statement, "using the Perfect to receive the Small," this refers to the reception prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, where names are opened up but the methods differ.
Furthermore, regarding the "distinct intention of the gradual," this refers to those within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* who understand the Perfect while practicing gradually; it does not apply to all.

Regarding "sameness and difference": although these three are not identical, they all take the eternal as their cause and take the eternal fruit as their ultimate refuge; because they abide in Great Nirvana, there is no difference between them.
Thus, the text says: "Although the cause is impermanent, the fruit is eternal. This is the meaning of the second instance; other cases follow this pattern.
"It can be known" (and so forth). Question:
Is the explanation of the five meanings in the chapter on "Clarifying the Essence" the same as that for "Clarifying the Thesis"? Answer: It is the same by analogy.
△ Second, clarifying the meaning of the thesis is divided into two parts: first, the headings and enumeration.
The school has three meanings: first, the fundamental basis of the school; second, the essential core of the school; and third, the auxiliary elements of the school.
Next, in the main explanation, the text is divided into three parts, the first of which is the fundamental basis of the school.

Regarding the fundamental basis of the school: all conditioned phenomena take the mind of Great Nirvana as their basis. When the basis is established, the Way arises; it is like having no main rope [to hold a net together].
The eyes do not establish [themselves] without skin or hair; they have no point of attachment. Because the mind of *nirvāṇa* is the root, its school is established.
As the text says.
△ Next, within the Essentials of the School:
As for the essential principles of practice, the core of these principles lies in constant cultivation.

When one meets with constancy, one can manifest that which is neither eternal nor impermanent—just as the seven celestial bodies revolve around the North Star, or as the myriad rivers flow into the Eastern Sea.
That the essence of practice likewise consists in constancy is precisely like this.
It is said that the North Star is the Pole Star, which does not move; the Eastern Sea is of a single salty taste, and thus the salty taste is used as a metaphor for constancy.
△ Third, among the auxiliary elements of the school.

"Assistance for the tenet" (*shōjo*) means that "assistance" (*jo*) refers to supportive power. That a tenet is constantly established depends upon assistance—whether assistance from persons, assistance from teachings, assistance from practice, or assistance from the Path.
Because one gains power through such assistance, it is called "assistance for the tenet."
It is said that "assistance" may refer to assistance by persons, meaning spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); or assistance by teaching, meaning the verbal teachings that explain;

or assistance by practice, meaning the cultivation of practices to bring them to completion; or assistance by the path, meaning the cultivation of the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) within the three teachings to assist in manifesting the universal and eternal.
This is explained in detail in the section on the "Aids to the Path" (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the *Zhi guan*.

Taken together, these three aspects constitute the meaning of the "explanation of names" (釋名). To focus specifically on the fundamental tenet is the meaning of the "treatise on the tenet" (論宗). To focus specifically on clarifying the essential core of the tenet is the meaning of the "tenet itself" (宗).
To focus specifically on clarifying the auxiliary elements of the tenet is the meaning of "function" (用). To differentiate these three from other dharma-gates is the meaning of the "teaching" (教).
△ Section Four: Explaining the Function of Nirvāṇa. This is divided into three parts: first, the enumeration; second, the explanation; third, the questions and answers.
Regarding the fourth part, the explanation of the function of nirvāṇa, there are three sections: 1) the fundamental function, 2) the appropriate function, and 3) the function of sovereign arising.

The first part is as stated in the text. △ Second, the explanation of "for oneself" is divided into three sections. First, the explanation of the primary function is divided into three parts: first, recounting the old interpretation; second, "there is another person below," which introduces the objections of others;

third, "now, furthermore," which provides the correct explanation. Regarding the first, the recounting of the old interpretation, there are two further divisions. First, the actual recounting of the views of the three masters.
Regarding the "Original Function," the former commentator Lingwei Xiaoliang first presented an old interpretation, stating:

"Within the midst of birth and death, there originally exists the nature of the true spirit (*tathatā-citta*), like a golden image wrapped in tattered silk that has fallen into deep mud. One with the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) seizes it, cleanses it, and unwraps it;
the golden image remains intact, and the body of the Buddha is complete with all its myriad virtues, yet it is [currently] obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*)."

If one can sever the delusions that cover [the mind], the Buddha-body manifests of itself; this is like the metaphors of the wrestler’s forehead jewel, the poor woman’s treasure store, the seven jewels in the well, and the vase and basin in the dark room—it is likewise so.
All of these are inherently present, and they possess this functional efficacy. Xīn'ān (Xin’an) recounts the interpretation of Xiǎoshān Yáo (Xiǎoshān Yuáo), which states:
"The mental consciousness of sentient beings is never severed; it is the true cause of Buddha-nature, which adheres to this."

Sentient beings who have not yet perfected the myriad virtues must necessarily possess the principle of attaining Buddhahood; taking this principle of certain attainment as the foundation is what constitutes its practical utility.
Kaishan and Zhuangyan state: "The Buddha-nature of the True Cause is a single dharma without dual principles;

it is only by way of 'original existence' and 'initial existence' that two periods are distinguished. If there is originally divine assistance, there is the principle of attaining the fruit; if one is able to practice cultivation..."
The Golden Heart thanks the seed; awakening arises and is named "the beginning. The principle of having a beginning has fundamentally existed from the outset.
△ Second, the citation of proofs consists of four parts within itself:
citing the Tathāgata-nature, the poor woman’s forehead jewel, the dark room, and so forth, to prove that [enlightenment] is inherently present.
The teacher Śāṇakavāsin cited this: "There is no curd within milk; it is only because curd is produced from milk that one says 'there is curd. Curd does not exist inherently;

it must depend on the warmth of fermenting agents and the planting [of conditions]. Likewise, when asked if there is oil in sesame seeds, he replied: 'There is oil, but oil must be obtained through pounding and pressing.'"
The first two [sections] are as stated in the text.
△ In the third section, it further cites that all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time shall, in the future, possess a body of pure adornment; this serves as proof.
The meaning of "possessing both" (*dang you shuang qu*) regarding the two textual passages does not differ from that of Master Yao.

As for what is meant by "possessing both," it refers simply to the fact that there is currently the *pratyaya-buddhadhātu* (causal Buddha-nature) and there will be the *viśuddha-alaṃkāra* (pure adornment);
this is called "possessing both."
△ Fourth, distinguishing between wood and stone.
Furthermore, if it were the case that those categories such as wood and stone lack the principle of attaining Buddhahood, then the inherent function [of sentient beings] would not exist;

yet sentient beings must inevitably become Buddhas. Thus, the present state is the cause, while this cause is inherently existent. The fruit is what begins to exist; the inherent existence is that which begins.
The principle of its existence is precisely the meaning of functional efficacy;
this is evident.
△ Next, within the refutation, there are three parts: first, the formal refutation of the three schools.

Someone raises an objection to the initial position: If one says that the fruit of Buddhahood already exists within the bodies of sentient beings, this entails the fallacy of the cause containing the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
For example, if excrement were already present in food, or if a child were already present in a young girl, why would they remain amidst afflictions and refuse to emerge?
Why would they not emit light or shake the earth? As the text says: "If one says..."

As for the first [position], why did [the Buddha] remain silent? It was precisely to refute this attachment. Next, we shall challenge the second [position]: the principle that there is a "principle of attaining Buddhahood" (*gotra*).

If this principle is permanent, does it constitute a continuity or is it immutably fixed? If it is a continuous permanence, how can it be called the "primordially existing principle of the Buddha-fruit"?
If it is an immutable permanence, then the fault of "the effect existing within the cause" (*satkāryavāda*) is identical to the previous refutation. Third...
If you say that what is originally possessed is also newly possessed, then it should also be originally permanent while simultaneously being impermanent.

If that which is originally possessed can only be permanent and cannot be impermanent, then "original possession" would simply be "original possession"; how could there be such a thing as "new possession"?
△ Furthermore, if [the two] were to run parallel from below;

and if there were both "original existence" (*pūrvabhāva*) and "existence with a beginning" (*ādyutpanna-bhāva*), then "permanence" (*nitya*) would also have to be impermanent. Since permanence and impermanence cannot coexist within permanence, how could there be "existence with a beginning" within original permanence?
Moreover, if there were both original existence and existence with a beginning, then the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*) would necessarily entail a "generating cause" (*janaka-hetu*).

If the revealing cause reveals that which is originally existent and eternal, while the producing cause produces that which begins to exist and is impermanent, and if one cannot obtain [the notion of] existence through characteristics,
then how can that which is originally existent now possess a beginning of existence?
△ Third: The Conclusion on the Losses Regarding the Heron and the Oyster.
It has long been the case that the heron and the oyster grapple with one another, each asserting its own right and denying the other’s;
all is as stated in the text.
△ Third, the correct explanation.

Now, this meaning shall be proclaimed and clarified: if one dogmatically adheres to the view that what exists inherently must exist in the future, this is not the tenet of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) nor the universal teachings;

rather, it is the intent of the four gates of the Distinct and Perfect [Vehicles]. Herein, "inherent existence" is the gate of affirmation (you-men), while "future existence" is the gate of negation (wu-men); taking both together is...

The gate of "both existence and non-existence" simultaneously discards [the views of] being and non-being; the gate of "neither existence nor non-existence" specifically rejects the partial adherence of other schools that lacks integration;
and the gate of "losing both principles" is what is refuted by the Perfect School. Why is this so? If one clings to the inherent function [of dharmas], it is like a carpenter measuring timber:
he uses what is curved for beams, what is straight for rafters, what is long for spears, and what is short for arrows.
The utility of what is inherently present is also like this. The Buddha then refuted it: "When grass and trees grow, they have no use as beams or arrows;

it is through the conditions of being fashioned by a craftsman that they obtain utility. If one cuts what is curved to make it straight, the curve has no use as a beam; if one stretches what is straight to make it curved, the straightness has no use as a crossbeam.
If one cuts what is long to make it a tally, the length has no use as a spear; if one breaks what is short to make it firewood, the shortness has no [use]."
Why do you so stubbornly cling to the notion that function exists inherently? The Sūtra states: "It is impossible for dharmas to exist throughout the three periods of time [simultaneously].
How can you so stubbornly cling to inherent existence? If the primary and secondary functions cannot be established, where is the superior function located?

If you merely focus on refutation, you will lose the opportunity to adapt to conditions. Why? Because the principle is neither past nor future, neither both past and future, nor even the negation of both past and future.

There are four benefits: some say that what is originally present (*mūla-bhava*) is precisely the constant application; some say that what is to come (*āgamiṣyat*) is precisely the non-constant application;

some say that both what is to come and what is original constitute the dual application of the constant and the non-constant; and some say that neither what is to come nor what is original constitutes the application of the "non-use" of the dual negation.
Since the original presence and the constant application encompass all phenomena, how could there not be the applications of the three gates? There are indeed the three gates.
Furthermore, it encompasses all dharmas; how could it be without an original basis? As for the constant functioning, the text states:

"Mahāparinirvāṇa is the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas"—this is precisely its meaning. This constitutes the Perfect Teaching’s discourse on these four functions in accordance with conditions, which brings about great benefit and differs from the old interpretations (and so forth).

The text consists of nine sections: first, clarifying the gate of establishing [the position] through fixed attachment; second, showing the characteristics of the gate of establishment from "originally existing" (*bennyū*) onwards;

third, clarifying the fault of partial reliance from "listing the schools" (*rekke*) onwards; fourth, refuting partiality by citing the Buddha from "the Buddha immediately" (*busoku*) onwards; fifth, refuting attachment by citing scripture from "the Dharma says" (*hōun*) onwards;

There are four sections: first, the title; second, the benefit obtained; third, the fundamental existence; fourth, the function of the gate of the lower illumination;
and fifth, the concluding summary of benefits. Regarding the initial statement, "Now I shall proclaim and illuminate," it simply means that I shall now manifest and reveal this meaning.

△ Second, regarding the utility [of the mirror], there are four sections: first, citing the differing views of the ancients; second, the refutation by "some people" and below; third, the formal explanation starting with "now I clarify" and below;

Second, regarding that which is to be utilized, we first present the ancient interpretations, which are threefold: 1. One interpretation states that the Principle lies beyond the myriad delusions;
one must eliminate the delusions entirely before it can be seen. This is illustrated by the metaphor of a pillar wrapped in ten layers of paper:

although nine layers may be removed, the pillar is still not visible; only when all are exhausted is it revealed. 2. Another cites the *Jianbei jing* (Sutra on the Gradual Preparation) to clarify that all wisdom is attained progressively.

Faman does not consider that both [the truth and the fruit] are realized simultaneously. Third, he says that while the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) can be known gradually, the Buddha-fruit can be attained suddenly.
Why is this? Because the ultimate is identical with the conventional; it is not a separate entity removed from it. Therefore, the ultimate truth can be known in stages.
However, because the Buddha-fruit transcends the realm of delusion and is not identical with birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it cannot be known gradually.
Regarding the first point, "the paper is heavy," this means the paper is dense, which can be used as a metaphor for the density of ignorance (*avidyā*). The second master’s view is easily understood.

Regarding the third point, "the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) can be known gradually," this means that by gradually destroying conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one perceives the ultimate truth part by part; therefore, it is said that it can be known gradually.

As stated in the text.

If you say that principle can be seen gradually, then if principle were divisible, it could be known part by part; yet since principle is perfectly pervasive and unobstructed...
Regarding gradual perception: if what was seen at first is called "seen later" and is no different from the latter [perception], it is not termed gradual perception;
if what was seen at first is not so designated, it is not termed sudden perception (and so forth).
Now, as for the principle that these [stages] are differentiated: even this objection raised by others is not entirely appropriate.
Why? If one penetrates to the contemplation of True Suchness from the very beginning, it is entirely undifferentiated.

However, if one speaks from the perspective of falling into the increase of wisdom, one must say they are differentiated, because there are forty-two distinct stages. In explaining this meaning, one must know this.

The *Avataṃsaka* says: "Those with many false discriminations perceive saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as distinct; they are deluded regarding the dharma of the sages and do not recognize the Unsurpassed."

Regarding this, there are three parts: first, the general discussion; second, the citation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; and third, the conclusion regarding the error of [the opponent's] position.

First, as for the separate discussion: it is proven that the initial mind is already a sudden contemplation. What discussion is there of naming it "sudden" only upon reaching the fruit? Therefore, [that position] is untenable. Next, he cites the *Avataṃsaka*.
Yan said: "If one discriminates between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as being different, this is delusion regarding the Dharma of the noble ones (ārya).

△ Third, the correct explanation has two parts. First, the faults are restated.
Now, it is clarified that various interpretations chase one another like water agitating a pearl, causing it to become obscured; yet the principle is neither distant nor near.

How could the wisdom that perceives the principle be gradual or sudden? If it were gradual or sudden, how could it be called "in accordance with principle"? It would be like a square entering a circle—they are utterly incompatible.

It is so. △ Next, from "according to principle" (*yathābhūta*) onwards, there is the formal explanation, which consists of three parts. First, it clarifies that the essence of wisdom and phenomena is a profound unity, being neither sudden nor gradual.
To understand according to the principle, and to understand such that one does not perceive characteristics within the principle but perceives only non-attainment—this is precisely attainment itself.

△ (At this point, there may be a textual omission; I now venture to supplement it: "The two types of causes" below indicate the application of causes and conditions for sentient beings, which is both gradual and sudden.)
Because there are causes and conditions, one may also attain [enlightenment] both gradually and suddenly.

Within this, there should be four propositions: gradual-gradual, gradual-sudden, sudden-gradual, and sudden-sudden.
The first, "gradual-gradual," refers to the causal stages of the three vehicles. "Gradual-sudden" refers to the fruition of the three vehicles.
"Sudden-gradual" refers to the causal stage of the Perfect Teaching (the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* school). "Sudden" refers to the fruition of the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching.
△ Second, the formal explanation is divided into five parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the subsequent further opening of one sentence into four sentences;
third, taking this one sentence as an example for the remaining three sentences; fourth, concluding the extensive explanation to refute partiality;
fifth, citing the text to prove that its function pervades the Dharma-realm.
Gradually, even "gradual and sudden" is not yet [the truth], let alone "sudden, gradual, and sudden"; even "sudden, gradual, and sudden" is not yet "sudden and sudden," let alone "sudden and sudden.

That the *Lotus Sūtra* extensively explains "sudden" and "gradual" means that within non-differentiation there is differentiation; that "sudden and sudden" means that within differentiation there is non-differentiation.

This is precisely the intent of clarifying the fundamental principle regarding the three kinds of cultivation and the three kinds of insight. This refers to the cultivation of the gradual and the sudden.
The "gradual and sudden vision" refers to the intent of indeterminate contemplation (*aniyata-bhāvanā*).

Regarding the initial mention of the "three kinds of cultivation" and so forth: in the preceding section of the text, the first refutation of impermanence while cultivating permanence represents the connection of the Perfect [Teaching] with the Shared [Teaching].
Subsequently, the sequence from the gradual to the sudden represents the specific intent of the successive [teachings]; thereafter, it is precisely within impermanence that...
To cultivate the "constant" (nitya) refers to those of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle].

△ Next, within the text, the gradual [approach] is further differentiated into four permutations: gradual cultivation and gradual seeing; gradual cultivation and sudden seeing; gradual cultivation and gradual-sudden [seeing]; and [the fourth permutation].
Regarding the view that cultivation is gradual while realization is both gradual and sudden:
those who take the realized persons of the Three Teachings as examples represent the "gradual cultivation and gradual realization" (jiànxiū jiànjiàn).

Those who have attained entry into the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and above represent the "gradual cultivation and sudden realization" (jiànxiū dùnjiàn). Those who are at the stage prior to entering [the stages] represent the "gradual cultivation and gradual-sudden realization" (jiànxiū jiàndùnjiàn), wherein the period prior to entry constitutes the gradual realization.

Abiding is termed "sudden seeing" and "gradual cultivation," not "sudden and gradual seeing. When one realizes suddenness and gradualness, at that time there is no characteristic of suddenness in the sudden, nor any characteristic of gradualness in the gradual;
this is because the essence of reality (li-ti) does not correspond to sudden or gradual seeing.
Having understood the meaning of this first phrase, the remaining three phrases can likewise be explained. Furthermore,
the four phrases concerning sudden cultivation and gradual seeing are the same, as are the four phrases concerning gradual cultivation and gradual/sudden seeing,
and the four phrases concerning neither sudden nor gradual cultivation.
One should know that the sixteen distinct phrases, arranged as four sets of four, reveal that the functions of the essence are manifold;

how could one interpret them as merely one or two types? As the text says: "A single wrestler of the royal house can match a thousand, for he excels a thousand through his various arts. Thus, it is "one person."
Daōan further said: "For example, just as the great earth and its grasses and trees are used by sentient beings, so too is my Dharma;
you should know that its utility is like that of grass and trees. By comparing it to the great strongman, one knows that its utility is not uniform."

△ Fourth, the "Old Treatise" (Jiùlùn) below: illuminating the objects [of cognition] constitutes four sections. First, the distinction between [the views] is established; second, the inquiry is raised as the reason for providing an explanation;
third, Penglai does not describe the characteristics of these differences; fourth, from "Now we clarify" onwards, the actual explanation is given.
The old treatise explains that the functions of illuminating objects differ.
The first point is as stated in the text.
△ Next, within the second question:
Question: In the mundane world, the three periods of time are in flux and the myriad objects come and go; how does the Buddha’s wisdom illuminate them?

If it follows the coming and going of objects, it would be subject to arising and ceasing and thus impermanent; if it does not follow the coming and going of objects, it would not correspond with those objects.
From this single question, seven different interpretations arise.

The question, "How does the Buddha's wisdom illuminate [all things]? intends to ask: Does the Buddha illuminate by pursuing what has gone and what has come, or does he illuminate without pursuing what has gone and what has come?
△ Third, the description of differing characteristics consists of seven sections in total; in each, one first presents the position and subsequently refutes it, as in the text.
It can be seen.

Yecheng Song said: "The fact that even those with great wisdom do not escape death and extinction, yet still experience the constant flow of thought-moments coming and going in pursuit of objects, is a present proof of the fault of one who, at the moment of death, suffers their tongue to rot and utters delirious speech."

Second, the interpretation that the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom is permanent while its function is impermanent, coming and going in accordance with objects—this interpretation also contradicts the sutra.
The sutra says: "If one has right view, it should be said that the Tathāgata is definitively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
why then would his essence be unconditioned while his function is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?"

Third, Guangzhai said: "If the wisdom of impermanence illuminates the realm of permanence yet does not follow that realm as being permanent, then how could the wisdom of permanence, when illuminating the realm of impermanence, possibly follow that realm as being impermanent? This, too, is untenable."
△ Fourth, regarding the nine periods within the four [realms]:

the meaning of the four acts illuminating the objects across the nine periods is clarified here. Although these objects exist in the future, they further possess the sense of being about to be present and about to be past;
now, as they actually arrive in the present and the past, I have already fully illuminated them all. Therefore, they are neither produced nor extinguished.
Furthermore, this is also untenable: when [a phenomenon] was still in the future, it was yet to be present;

not yet being present, it then comes into the present and becomes truly present. Once it has been illuminated as truly present, one should know that it has already ceased; how could it not be subject to arising and ceasing?
The phrase "that which has now come to exist in the present" means that when a momentary mind arises, the objects of the future manifest within the present mind;
this is termed "presently existing. That which has already ceased in a moment is termed "not yet past.
Therefore, it illuminates all things within the present.
△ Regarding the fifth, the simultaneous retroactive illumination (*pratyaṅgama-āloka*):

The meaning of the simultaneous retroactive illumination is that when the Tathāgata’s path welcomes the supreme awakening, at the very first thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), he simultaneously retroactively illuminates all phenomena from their initial flow [into saṃsāra] until his subsequent attainment of Buddhahood;
thus, he completes the illumination of all things. Subsequently, the myriad phenomena themselves possess coming and going.
I do not update my perception; rather, I perceive all things as they were when the Son of Heaven first ascended the throne, simultaneously bestowing the established laws.

If later generations violate them, they shall be punished according to the gravity of their offense, and no further laws need be enacted. This too is impossible: how could the Buddha’s wisdom, which illuminates objects, ever cease for even a moment?
To suddenly claim that it illuminates at first but thereafter does not illuminate at all—even if this were so, it would ultimately fail to correspond with the nature of objects.
As for what is called "retroactive illumination," it simply means "anticipatory illumination.
△ Sixth, regarding the Kai-sen school:

The sixth [master] of the Kai-sen school says that when the Buddha was still on the path of cause, while guiding and inspiring the initial resolve, he was already able to illuminate numerous objects horizontally and illuminate them vertically.
After a certain period, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), where in a single thought-moment there is horizontal illumination of a hundred dharmas and vertical illumination for a hundred moments;

in the second stage, a thousand dharmas, and so on until the Buddha-stage, where in a single thought-moment there is horizontal illumination of ten thousand dharmas and vertical illumination for ten thousand moments—like a mirror suspended high upon a platform.
Yet even this cannot avoid the difficulty of impermanence, for it is impossible for a reflection to exist in the mirror that was previously non-existent and only subsequently comes to be.
Regarding "a hundred moments," this refers to the duration of the arising and ceasing of mental conditions (*ālambana*).
△ Seventh, the "Sublime Flavor" (*rasa*):

To further illustrate the seven sublime flavors, we borrow the analogy of empty space; all things exist within emptiness, yet emptiness itself neither arises nor perishes, for it is the things themselves that come and go.
Coming here [to this position] is likewise not correct; for how could the numinous cognition of Buddha-wisdom be the same as insentient emptiness?
As the text says.
△ Fourth, "Now, to clarify below," is the actual explanation, which has three parts: first, the actual explanation; second, "Furthermore, Kai-she... is the re-statement.

Regarding the third point, "Explaining the Buddha’s Wisdom," in the following section on resolving difficulties, it is now clarified that within the Tripiṭaka Teaching, the two truths are not mutually identical; therefore, the two wisdoms each illuminate their respective objects, which is why various interpretations are as clamorous as these.
Furthermore, in the Shared Teaching, the two truths are mutually identical, and thus the two wisdoms are both two and non-two—such [distinctions] do not even exist there.
This dispute is even more so when it concerns the three truths being identical to the one truth and the one truth being identical to the three truths;

the three wisdoms being identical to the one wisdom and the one wisdom being identical to the three wisdoms; and the single illumination being the illumination of all, and the illumination of all being the single illumination—wherein neither "one" nor "all" applies in an inconceivable manner.
How could there possibly be such a trivial and shallow exchange of questions and answers?
How much more so when the three truths are identical to the one truth? When illuminating impermanence, impermanence itself is permanence;
it is also neither permanence nor impermanence. When illuminating permanence, permanence itself is neither permanence nor impermanence.

As for these subtle and shallow questions and answers, they are as slight and shallow as the teachings questioned by the seven masters previously; yet the benefit derived from them is likewise [profound].

However. △ Next, the second section reiterates the middle [part] in two parts: first, the opening of the goodness; second, the clarification of its sequence and interpretation. The first part further has two sections:
first, clarifying that the wisdom and the object of the fruition stage are mutually merged.
Furthermore, Kai-shan explains that when the Buddha-wisdom illuminates the Truth, it merges with the Truth such that there is no longer any distinction between wisdom and its object;
the essence of wisdom and the objective realm of Truth are entirely non-different.
△ Next, regarding the "stages" (bhūmi), the following clarifies four distinct propositions based on these stages.
To distinguish according to stages: ordinary beings neither penetrate nor realize; the sages within the causal stage realize but do not penetrate;
and the Buddha-fruit both penetrates and realizes.

Regarding this, as for the statement that "the sages within the causal stage realize but do not penetrate," one should immediately refute it by asking: "Since they have already realized, why [do they not penetrate]?"
"Because it is not dark or deluded... (and so forth).
△ Next, the explanation has two parts; first, clarifying that the essence of wisdom is distinct [from the object].

The second explanation states: "Buddha-wisdom is spiritual cognition (*ling-zhi*), whereas the True Truth (*zhen-di*) is non-cognition (*wu-zhi*); since these two essences are distinct, how could they possibly [be identical]?"
Furthermore, although there is both knowing and non-knowing, once their convergence is perfected, it is designated as "mystery" (*ming*); how could there be a mystery distinct from this convergence?
△ Next, following the section on the Seal of Wisdom (*huiyin*), two proofs are cited.

The *Huiyin Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom) states: "The profound is not profound; the quiescent is not quiescent. The *Zhaolun* (Treatise by Sengzhao) likewise employs the phrase "the profound essence and the quiescent body.
△ Third, the present school’s refutation, which is divided into three parts: first, the concessionary objection.

Now, if you argue that the Buddha’s true wisdom is dark and identical with reality such that it does not differ from reality, then his conventional wisdom should likewise be dark and identical with the conventional such that it does not differ from the conventional;
yet, although the Buddha knows illusions, he is not an illusory person.
△ Next, from "If that were so" onwards, the faults are refuted:

If that were so, although the Buddha knows the conventional, he cannot be identical with the conventional; and although the Buddha is identical with the ultimate, he cannot be identical with the ultimate.
One should not maintain such a doctrine of being identical with the ultimate or identical with the conventional.
△ Third, the critique regarding the failure to penetrate reality:
If one does not penetrate reality, one remains at the level of the two vehicles; if one does not penetrate the conventional, one remains within the realm of ordinary beings.
How, then, can this be the functioning of Buddha-wisdom? (etc.)
△ Third, the arising of activity shall pervade the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the third, the arising of sovereign activity pervades the Dharma-realm extensively; it cannot be detailed in full. The text says:
"For example, just as all grasses and trees upon the great earth serve the needs of sentient beings, so too is my Dharma. One should know that its supreme functions are immeasurable and boundless."
△ Next, the chapters are opened for individual explanation. Within this, there are two parts: first, the headings and enumeration of the chapters; second, the detailed exposition.

For now, we shall rely on three types of applications: 1. the inconceivable application; 2. the application of the two birds flying together; and 3. the application of the dual inclusion of good and evil, as well as the heterodox and the orthodox.

The initial statement regarding "two birds flying together" means that when a practitioner perceives impermanence, this begins from the first arousal of the bodhicitta and continues until the year of equal enlightenment;
even when a fraction of ignorance remains, it is still termed "impermanence. Therefore, from beginning to end, both are designated by the name "flying together."
△ Next, the explanation of the text is divided into three parts. First, regarding the "inconceivable," there are three sections: first, the heading; second, the citation of previous interpretations;
third, the actual explanation below. As for the "inconceivable function": [The text continues with the explanation of the inconceivable function.]
The first part is as the text states.
△ Second, regarding the summary of the seven schools, in each individual explanation, the interpretations of those schools are first presented, followed by the current school’s refutation of them.
There are seven traditional explanations. The first says: "It causes others to see Mount Sumeru enter a mustard seed;

in reality it does not enter, but only those who are to be saved can perceive it. This interpretation is untenable. If it does not actually enter, what would one call this supernormal power (*abhijñā*)?

Second, regarding the entry into reality: if it is merely by the Buddha’s supernatural power that the large is contracted to become small and the small is expanded to become large, this too is untenable.
If that were so, it would mean that the large contains the small; how then can it be said that the small contains the large?

Regarding the three types of understanding, since one cannot know whether one has entered [the state] or not— given that this is inconceivable (*acintya*)— how can it be definitively judged as either "entered" or "not entered"?
Furthermore, if even this is inconceivable, and all stages above the fruit of Buddhahood are likewise inconceivable such that none should be understood,
why then do you say that everything else is understandable, while this single point alone is said to be unknown?
Fourth, if they exist, they would mutually obstruct one another; yet since both the small and the large are empty, they are mutually accommodated. This too is untenable.
If both were equally possible, what would there be to discuss regarding "entering," for then there would be no distinction between large and small.
The first four masters are as stated in the text. △ Fifth Master:
Within the great nature of the five elements there is a small nature, and within the small there is a great nature; thus, the great nature of a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru.
This small nature is likewise untenable; if one clings to a fixed nature, the error is identical to that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and it also resembles the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, this is merely a case of the large containing the small—how can this be called "the small containing the large"?
Regarding the statement that "the large contains the nature of the small," this refers to the refutation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the section on matter (*rūpa*).

As for the remark that "the error is the same as that of the non-Buddhists," it is identical to the fourfold nature theory (*caturvidha-svabhāva*) of the *ṛṣis*. Furthermore, its resemblance to the *Abhidharma* is due to the *Abhidharma* tenet that dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*).
△ Commentary on the Sixth Ground:
In the commentary on the Sixth Ground, the Great [emptiness] has no characteristic of greatness, yet it does not lack the Greatness of non-characteristic;

the Small has no characteristic of smallness, yet it does not lack the Smallness of non-characteristic. By means of the Small of non-characteristic, one accommodates the Great of non-characteristic; the Great of non-characteristic, in turn, enters back into [the Small].
To say that "the small is formless" is also untenable. Since "large" and "small" are fundamentally characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), how can there be large or small if one speaks of being formless?
If there were large or small, it would necessarily entail having characteristics; yet if it is definitively formless, it would be identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
It can be seen.

△ Seven, Xinghuang: Xinghuang says that all dharmas are fundamentally without [distinctions of] large or small; they are merely provisional names established through mutual dependence, and "large" is spoken of as a conventional designation.
If one provisionally posits the small as large and the large as small—where the small is both large and small, and the large is both small and large—then they might be able to coexist.
Yet even this is impossible. The large does not become large of itself; it is made large by depending on the small. The small does not become small of itself;

it is made small by depending on the large. This falls into the error of "other-nature" (parabhāva). If even self-nature (svabhāva) cannot accommodate such distinctions of large and small, how could they possibly coexist?
How could their distinct natures and differing dimensions possibly be mutually compatible?

As for the statement that "all things originally lack [intrinsic nature] until they are provisionally established through causes and conditions," this means that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and are both provisional and devoid of substantial reality.
Because they are provisional and devoid of substantial reality, they are able to interpenetrate one another.

△ Third, the correct explanation is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the mutual identity of the inconceivable phenomena and principle; second, from "one nature" onwards, clarifying the inconceivable pervasiveness;
third, from "that which is called" onwards, explaining the characteristics of the application of the heterodox and the orthodox.
Now it is clarified that the small is not small by itself, nor does it arise from the large; likewise, the large is not large by itself, nor does it arise from the small.
Because they are dependent on causes and conditions, the small and the large are neither separate from the large nor separate from the small. They do not exist within, without, or in between the two;
nor do they possess permanence of their own accord. This is inconceivable. The large is also like this. By thoroughly penetrating this principle, one acts in accordance with reality.
However, only those who are truly ready for deliverance perceive that the inconceivable height and breadth of Mount Sumeru enter into the inconceivably minute space of a mustard seed;
this is called "entering the inconceivable small with the inconceivable large.
Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one is able to establish great significance, as explained at length in the sūtra (and so forth).
The initial statement, "Now, to clarify up to 'causes and conditions' (hetu-pratyaya)," means that whether things are large or small, they all arise from causes and conditions; yet,

because they are identical to the dharma-nature (dharmatā) despite arising from causes and conditions, they are able to interpenetrate one another, as is explained extensively at the beginning of the fifth chapter of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), in the section on "Destroying Pervasiveness."
Superficially, it clarifies that the inconceivable function resides after the Way; in reality, this principle extends even to such examples as good and evil, heterodoxy and orthodoxy, and so forth.
△ Third, regarding the functions of heterodoxy and orthodoxy, there are three parts: first, clarifying the dual application of heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
