Next, the "floating bag" refers to the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā); the "white bones" refers to the training in meditative concentration (samādhi-śikṣā); and the "eight [sufferings]" refers to the training in wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā).
...Furthermore, next is the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

As for the "Shared Teaching," it is that which is studied in common by the three vehicles (*triyāna*), through which both the near and the far are universally accessible; if one can advance forward, one may likewise attain liberation.

The Mahāyāna Dharma is such that when a bodhisattva practices with the mind of Great Nirvāṇa, they immediately accomplish the holy conduct (*āryacaryā*). This is precisely the meaning of the scriptural passage:

"Understanding suffering as being without suffering, yet there is the True Truth," and so on, up to "understanding the Path as being without a path, yet there is the True Truth. This is the literal sense of the text.

Regarding the near and far [distances] common to the study of the Three Vehicles: those of dull faculties find the near [destination], passing through the illusory city; those of sharp faculties reach the far [destination], penetrating to the precious site.
Therefore it is said: "If one can advance forward, one may also attain departure"—this refers precisely to such a person.
△ Third, the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*).
As for the "Separate Teaching," it is distinct in that it pertains exclusively to Bodhisattvas and is not shared with those of the Two Vehicles;

its practice and principle are not within their realm, and thus it is the unique Dharma of Bodhisattvas alone. If one cultivates this with the mind of Great Nirvāṇa, it becomes the Holy Practice (*āryacaryā*), as stated in the Sūtra.

Suffering has immeasurable characteristics; when analyzed and calculated, it is of immeasurable kinds, which are not known even by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—and this applies even to the Path itself—such is the meaning of the text.
This can be understood.
△ Fourth, within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
As for the Perfect Teaching: it is principle within phenomena; one teaching is all teachings, and all teachings are one teaching; it is neither one nor many.
All that is inconceivable follows the Buddha’s own intention; this is the realm of the Buddha and is not known by the two vehicles or those of the lower stages.
As the sutra states: "It is neither suffering nor a truth that possesses reality, and so on, up to it is neither the path nor a truth that possesses reality.
This is called the Single Ultimate Truth (*eka-satya*); such is the meaning of the text.

"Phenomena are identical to principle" means that one realizes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves eternally abiding, and furthermore, that one realizes the distinct aspects of the conventional and the ultimate are themselves the eternally abiding principle;
therefore, it is said they are "identical. Furthermore, "one teaching as all teachings" refers to opening up all provisional teachings and the like.
△ Third, the summary into five parts: First, the initial summary gradually becomes complete; second, there is the lower summary where the initial mind is sudden;
third, this sutra’s lower summary is judged [as such]; fourth, "if categorized as below," the distinctions in names are clarified; fifth, "if exemplified by below," the examples are explained.
The cultivation of the Bodhisattva’s mind of Great Nirvana is precisely the Perfect Mind;

taking the Perfect Mind as the foundation, one practices among the various deeds from the shallow to the deep, ceasing only upon reaching the ultimate limit—just as when a vajra is cast and it comes to rest upon hitting the boundary.
One should know that the single meaning of the Holy Practice is precisely the teaching of both gradual and sudden, also called the Gradual-Perfect Teaching; this is merely one type within the text.
The initial statement that one "reaches the ultimate and stops" refers to the ultimate being *miao-jue* (wondrous enlightenment).
Furthermore, there is a single practice that is the practice of the Tathāgata, namely the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa;
this is where the journey begins, where all is sudden, and where all is complete. All dharmas enter therein, and all streams are salty—none are not the ocean of nature (*dharmadhātu*).
There is no difference between gradual perfection (*jiànyuán*) and sudden perfection (*dònyuán*); it is only called "gradual" because it proceeds through the gates of sequential stages.

This present sutra, however, possesses both textual accounts and is named according to its preeminent quality; that is, it is the teaching of perfect suddenness (*yuántùn*), which is the most honored and supreme among all teachings.

If one classifies them by their common names, there are four collections (*piṭaka*); the three collections are the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the miscellaneous collection (*kṣudraka-piṭaka*) is the general category, and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is the specific category.
The circular [collection] is the Buddha-piṭaka; as it can encompass those above and below, the Buddha-piṭaka is the foremost.
△ Regarding the five examples for explanation:

if one applies the four propositions to the Three Baskets, the Tripitaka is "that which is heard" (śruta); the Shared [Teaching] is "that which is heard but not heard"; the Distinct [Teaching] is "that which is not heard but heard";
and the Perfect [Teaching] is "that which is neither heard nor not heard. This may be understood by applying the same logic to "birth after birth" (*jāti-jāti*) and so forth.
It is said that "not hearing" means not hearing. That the birth of *paricchinna* (segmented existence) does not arise is one instance of not hearing;

that the birth of *pariṇāma* (transformative existence) does not arise is another instance of not hearing. Furthermore, that the birth of the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*) does not arise is one instance of not hearing, and that the birth of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇaguṇa*) does not arise is another instance of not hearing. Therefore, it is called "not hearing, not hearing."
△ Fifth, explaining the "flavors" (rasa) in four sections: first, explaining the intent of the preceding metaphors; second, from "If at the beginning...

onwards, explaining the arising of the Dharma and its metaphors to reveal the characteristics of the five flavors; third, from "Now, as for the multitude of beings... onwards, concluding by showing the provisional wisdom of the same essence and the path of teaching through the five periods to benefit sentient beings;
fourth, from "The five flavors... onwards, pointing to the extensive [commentaries] and correlating them with the five chapters.
At the beginning, there are again two parts; first, the statement of the intent.

Regarding the "five flavors," these refer to the five kinds of bovine flavors used as a direct metaphor for the sequence of the teachings. One should not interpret them according to a hierarchy of shallow or deep;
if one were to claim that the former is shallow and the latter is deep, such an interpretation would be incorrect.

△ Next, the text states that the following citations provide further proof, which is twofold: first, proving that the four flavors are not shallow; second, proving that the *amṛta* (clarified butter) is not deep.
The text says: "The physician diagnoses the King’s illness and determines that he must take milk," and further: "Once one has obtained milk and curd, there is nothing else required."
That which has no requirements is true liberation; true liberation is great *nirvāṇa*.
How could this be shallow? A scripture states: "It is like mixing water and milk; even if left for a month, it will never turn into curd.
But if a single drop of the juice of the *pārijāta* tree is cast into it, it immediately becomes curd. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this. If originally..."
As for why [the existence of] things depends upon conditions in this way, the analogy of curd is not to be taken lightly. The text says:
"For example, sweet butter is endowed with eight flavors; Great Nirvāṇa is also like this. One should know that this butter serves as a profound illustration."
The initial statement that "the analogy is profound" refers to the ghee of *amṛta* (clarified butter); therefore, it cannot be considered shallow.
The text states that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are like *amṛta*; such *amṛta* cannot be described as merely profound.
△ Next, the explanation of the relationship between the Dharma and the parable is divided into two parts. First, regarding the rejection of fixed attachments:
if one were to insist that the initial flavor is necessarily shallow and the subsequent flavor is necessarily deep, it would obstruct the text and harm the meaning.
△ Second, the explanation beginning with "If one acts... consists of five textual sections.

If one provides an interpretation according to the sequential order of the meaning, there is no fault. "The cow" is a metaphor for the Buddha, whose great awakening is luminous, radiant, and perfectly realized.
Just as blood transforms into milk and is fully present within the cow, the flowing forth of milk from the cow is a metaphor for the Buddha’s initial teaching.
That is, from the site of the Dharma-realm of tranquil extinction, the teachings of the Dharma-realm flow forth. The various bodhisattvas are like... [the calves].
Just as when the sun first rises, it shines first upon the high mountains, it is said that "milk comes forth from the cow.
Next, "curds come forth from the milk" refers to those of lesser capacity who are unable to receive [the profound truth], being like the deaf or the mute.

To conceal his immeasurable divine virtues and manifest a body sixteen feet tall, he covers the *tathāgatagarbha* and teaches only the Tripiṭaka, providing the Dharma that the poor delight in according to their suitability.

The Chapter on Expedient Means (Upāya) generally establishes the attainment of sainthood; therefore, after the *Avataṃsaka*, the "Small" [teachings] of the Three Piṭakas are explained next, just as curd follows immediately after milk.

Next, the production of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) from curd is a metaphor for how, following the Three Piṭakas, the Great [Vehicle] rebukes the Small, crushing its tendency toward premature realization.
"Defeated seeds and ruined roots are without birth and without function; 'first giving and later taking back' is like making fresh butter from curdled milk.

Next, 'extracting clarified butter from fresh butter' is a metaphor for the period following the Vaipulya [sūtras], wherein one entrusts the task and receives the wealth, causing the śrāvakas to turn their teaching to instruct the bodhisattvas."

Next, the emergence of *sarpirmanda* (the finest clarified butter) from *ghṛta* (matured butter) is a metaphor for the stage following *prajñā*, wherein the treasure is entrusted, the nature is determined, and the prediction of Buddhahood is bestowed.
Thus the text says: "Eight thousand *śrāvakas* receive the prediction of Buddhahood within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
they perceive the *tathāgatagarbha* as one who has harvested in autumn and stored away in winter, having nothing further to do. That which has nothing further to do is precisely the ultimate.
All may be understood.

△ Third, the conclusion and demonstration is divided into three parts: first, concluding the skillful means of the five periods; second, clarifying the merit of the opening and revealing through the words "Now this sutra...
and so forth; third, concluding with praise through the words "Various kinds... and so forth.
Now, because sentient beings do not see the Buddha-nature, the Wisdom-Hand points and gestures, sometimes delivering great teachings and sometimes small ones;
sometimes speaking with reprimand and sometimes speaking to transform and instruct; or speaking of the fixed nature of beings.

If sentient beings were to see the Buddha-nature, then [the Buddha] would rest beneath the twin trees, his pointing and gesturing would be finished, his teaching would cease, the flow of the two rivers of Dharma would be exhausted, and it would be like a cow that has yielded all its milk.
The teaching of all Buddhas culminates in the attainment of the nature of reality (darśana-svabhāva) at the stage of *tattva-ghṛta* (the finest clarified butter).
The initial mention of "two rivers" refers to the two rivers of afflictions (*kleśa*) and nirvana.
This present sutra represents the final teaching; it is likened to *tattva-ghṛta*, wherein all medicinal herbs are contained within it.
By praising its vertical height while it lies horizontally across the four flavors, this sutra praises the inconceivable nature of the teaching in various places;
this is merely a praise for the supreme, wondrous milk of the two characters "Ever-Abiding" (nitya), which is the final, newly perfected, and most complete teaching—
the exquisite flavor of *amṛta* (ghee).
△ Third, regarding the summary of praise:
These various names and titles refer to but a single Dharma; this single Dharma is none other than the Teacher of Buddhas and the Mother of all Bodhisattvas.

It is something that the eloquence of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot fully proclaim, so how could the thousand tongues of ordinary people ever understand its exaltation? How much less could the hundred blind ones of the Two Vehicles?
Regarding "the one who can dance with the hands":
she is called the Mother of Bodhisattvas because the Buddha is able to give birth to all bodhisattvas; "dancing" means "to rub.

The meaning of the five flavors is fully explained in the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra). Furthermore, from the increase of one up to five, this summarizes all the various explanations.

The meaning of the title is as follows: if it focuses exclusively on the five [aggregates], it constitutes the "essence" (tǐ); if it focuses exclusively on the five, it constitutes the "establishment of various names and characteristics" (míngxiàng), which is the "thesis" (zōng);
if it focuses exclusively on refuting [opposing views], it constitutes the "function" (yòng); and if it analyzes their characteristics, it constitutes the "teaching" (jiào).
These may be inferred from the preceding [explanations] and need not be explained in detail (etc.).

the Śramaṇa Lokakṣema from the Yuezhi country translated one version in Luoyang titled *Banniepan* (Parinirvāṇa).

The *Huanjing* (Scripture of the Huan) in two fascicles, forming the second section. During the Yuanjia era of Emperor Huan, the Śramaṇa An Shigao from the country of Parthia—having originally been a crown prince who renounced his kingdom to leave home, and whose primary vocation was traveling abroad to propagate the Way—arrived at the capital city of Luoyang carrying his mendicant’s staff.
He translated this work, originally titled the *Xiaobanniepan* (Minor Mahāparinirvāṇa), in one fascicle.
Section Three of the Chengbu (Establishment Section): Translated by the Śramaṇa An Faxian from the Western Regions during the Huangchu era of Emperor Wu of the Cao Wei dynasty.

Fourth: During the Huangwu era of Eastern Wu, there was a lay practitioner from the Yuezhi kingdom surnamed Zhi and named Daoqian.

The monk Zì Gōngmíng first arrived in Luoyang and later traveled to the region south of the Yangtze River, where he translated one version titled *Xiǎo bānnièpán* (Minor Parinirvāṇa) in two fascicles;

Translated at Daochang Monastery; one volume, also titled *Fangdeng Niepan*, forming the sixth section.

Seventh: [Translated] during the Taishi era of Emperor Wu of the Western Jin.

In that year, the Śramaṇa Dharmakṣaya (translated into Chinese as Fǎhù) from the country of Yuezhi first arrived in Dūnwāng, subsequently traveled to the capital, and later went to Jiangzuō, where he translated one version consisting of two fascicles titled the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Eighth: During the Northern Liáng dynasty, Juqu Mèngxùn occupied Hexī with his capital at Gūzāng County. Xuán...

In the beginning of the [Shi] era, there was the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema from India (translated into Chinese as Fǎfēng). He entered the monastic order at the age of six and could recite ten thousand words daily.
Initially, he studied the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) according to the Hīnayāna;

later, he encountered the White-Headed Meditation Master (*śvetakeśa-dhyānācārya*), who instructed him in the Mahāyāna. For ten months they debated, yet Dharmakṣema refused to comply, saying to the Meditation Master: "Is there perhaps a sūtra..."
Can he be seen? The Chan Master Zhi initially taught him the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, which he accepted with faith.
At that time, he was skilled in the wondrous incantations of the Tripiṭaka and was known by the people as a "Great Incantation Master.

Initially, he brought with him the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, as well as the Sanskrit manuscripts of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and other various scriptures.
At night, fearing he might lose his pillow, Śāṅkara lay down; however, a divine being pulled the *Kṣānti* (the scripture) from beneath him so that it fell to the ground.

This happened three times, at which point a voice from the air said: "This is the Vajra-liberation, the secret treasury of all Buddhas. Why are you in such haste to use it as a pillow? Why do you suddenly use the *Kṣānti* as a pillow?
Startled and filled with shame, Śāṅkara apologized and subsequently hung the Sanskrit manuscript upon a tall tree. Indeed, there it remained.
A band of thieves came at night intending to steal the scriptures; they exerted all their strength together to lift them, but in the end were unable to move them.
At dawn, the Tripitaka Master carried them away himself. When the thieves saw this together, they called him a sage, feeling ashamed and repentant.
Eventually, he reached Guzang, where he was detained by Ju Mengxun, the King of Hexi, who earnestly requested that he remain to translate the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The original Sanskrit manuscript began from the first ten fascicles up to the *Mahāsāṃghika-parivarta* (大眾品) of the *Bodhyanga-sūtra*.

Because the Tripitaka Master was slightly deficient in his knowledge, he traveled to the kingdom of Khotan and obtained the middle ten fascicles, which he translated up to the *Śiśu-carita-parivarta* (嬰兒行品).

As the *Bodhyanga-sūtra* was still incomplete, he again dispatched an envoy to the kingdom of Khotan to obtain the remaining portions; once these were translated, the work was complete and titled the *Mahā-*.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, forty fascicles; Ninth Section Completed.
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the śramaṇa Zhimeng of Yongzhou personally traveled to the Western Regions to seek the True Dharma.

Carrying various Sanskrit manuscripts, he arrived at the state of Xiliang and translated one version, titled the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in twenty fascicles; Tenth Section Completed. [Recorded by] Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty.
In the Jianyuan era, the Indian śramaṇa Guṇabhadra (translated into Chinese as Gōngdéxián) translated one version at Xinsi Monastery in Jingzhou;
its title is the *Niyue jing* (one fascicle). Number eleven:
in the first year of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi, the Western country śramaṇa Buddhayaśas (translated into Chinese as Juémíng) [translated it] at Xiangzhou.
One version titled *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* in five fascicles, Section Twelve:
the *Nāma-guṇa-sūtra* and the *Parideva-sūtra*, which are merely different translations of the same text as the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Thirteen:
one version titled *Catur-dāraka-sūtra* in three fascicles, translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta and Dharmagupta.

Consequently, they were allowed to spread. In the first year of the Tiancè Wansu era of the Great Zhou dynasty, he was commanded by imperial edict to compile these scriptures and include them in the catalog.
The text currently being expounded belongs to the eighth among the fourteen previously translated works in the northern [division].
The forty-fascicle collection translated by Kumārajīva is completed.

why then do both the preceding and following sections contain the full-length text, such as the Tathāgata’s discourse on the "Stealing Dog" in six fascicles, which is the full-length version of Kāśyapa’s inquiry regarding the "Stealing Dog"?

I have pulverized this text until it is like dust; yet, out of reverence, I have not dared to omit anything, but have merely removed the substance to preserve the ornament.
